We developed a novel algorithm and showed that it achieves the theoretical limit for sample efficiency in this setting. Furthermore, we found that unless our algorithm uses the suboptimal trajectories in a meaningful way, it cannot reach this optimal bound. We designed and implemented the algorithm and compared it to other sophisticated implementations under the same conditions. Our results indicate that our method significantly surpasses the competition and yields substantial improvements over baselines both in simulated and real-world robot experiments.

Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, confirming the benefits of inter-agent knowledge exchange in the absence of external supervision.

This paper proposes a metric function that yields an optimal performance on average, which significantly reduces decoding computations while maintaining superior error-correction performance for polarization-adjusted convolutional codes. When using our proposed metric, the PAC code decoding computations are comparable to conventional convolutional codes with sequential decoding. Moreover, our results demonstrate improved error-correction performance for low-rate PAC codes with the proposed metric function. We show that using the polarized cutoff rate as the bias in our metric function reduces the risk of incorrect path selection during decoding, exponentially decreasing as the incorrect path depth increases. We also prove and validate the Pareto distribution of PAC code computation complexity. Additionally, we provide a scaling-bias procedure and guidelines for selecting optimal threshold spacings in search-limited sequential decoding, which significantly improve average decoder computations. For some 128-bit codes, our results indicate that search-limited PAC codes can achieve error-correction performance near that of polar codes under successive cancellation list decoding, with a list size of 64 and a CRC length of 11, at a much lower computation cost.

Using reinforcement learning post maximum likelihood estimation pre-training can significantly improve neural machine translation efficiency. Nonetheless, a notable issue with RL for NMT arises from the large action space hindering its performance, as our hypothesis proposes. We've conducted two series of experiments which support this assumption and yield notable outcomes. Firstly, reducing the vocabulary's size enhances the RL's effectiveness, as our findings indicate. Furthermore, a notable improvement can be observed when the action space is reduced without changing the vocabulary, as validated by multiple metrics including BLEU scores, semantic similarity and human assessment. Our research discovered that initializing the final fully connected layer with a layer that generalizes action similarities resulted in substantial RL performance gains, averaging 1.5 BLEU points improvement.

A novel, markerless extrinsic calibration system is introduced that relies on real-world depth camera data rather than simulation or fiducial markers. Our system leverages machine learning to automatically develop and utilize real-world models for identifying and positioning the end-effector, predicting object rotation, and pinpointing critical points in a single image frame. A mathematical transformation and a keypoint-matching algorithm allow us to accurately estimate end-effector pose based on rotation and keypoint data. Enhanced system robustness is achieved through a combination of advanced algorithms, including the iterative closest point method, multi-frame processing, filtering, and outlier detection. Results show our method's calibration and pose estimation capabilities can be as precise as sub-centimeters and sub-degrees with minimal and unseen test poses; we have also found that incorporating data from just one optimal pose yields comparable accuracy.

This study introduces two key concepts, quasi-finitely separating maps and quasiapproximate identities, which form the basis for the definitions of QFS-spaces and quasicontinuous maps. Building upon these definitions, various properties and characteristics of QFS-spaces are investigated. Key findings include: Firstly, any QFS-space is inherently a quasicontinuous space; secondly, closed subspaces, as well as quasicontinuous projection spaces, derived from QFS-spaces are themselves QFS-spaces; thirdly, continuous retracts of QFS-spaces possess the same characteristic and specific types of QFS-space retracts can be constructed; lastly, upper power spaces of continuous QFS-spaces correspond to FS-spaces.

The rise of partisanship seems to be rising across various metrics including voter behavior and online engagement. Research into the Web's influence on polarization has produced several key findings in the past. To build on existing research and gain deeper insights, we've studied browsing habits of thousands of users along with their online interactions with news sources. Our results reveal that users' online exposure to news sources follows distinct ideological patterns where they consistently spend more time browsing news aligned with their own viewpoint. Moreover, we've identified clear partisan groups within the broader online population based on shared browsing habits. Ultimately, we examined the impact of user decision-making on online polarization, and we've uncovered substantial evidence indicating users' deliberate actions can contribute significantly to the amplification of partisan divisions.

We examine the Lehnert and Schweitzer proof that the word problem for Thompson's group V has a non-context-free property. We further prove this word problem to be equivalent to the complement of a combined cyclic variant of several context-free languages, and for some of its generators, the combined cyclic variant of four deterministic context-free languages is sufficient. This relationship reveals that the time complexity of solving V's word problem deterministically is no more than quadratically scaling with input size.

The study of open quantum systems under periodic driving forces is highly captivating 
because, in most cases, they achieve a non-equilibrium steady state, which is
marked by a constant current. In this study, we examine discrete time-driven
dynamics in the laboratory using a single photon system that is linked to its surroundings.
Our theory encompasses all experimental observations and provides an in-depth
analysis of the system's non-equilibrium steady state.
Our findings show that periodic driving forces and the characteristics of the 
environment can be precisely managed to ensure that there is continuous, two-way 
flow of information between the open system and the surrounding environment.

We explore how several established recurrent operators including curvature, Ricci, Jacobi, shape, and Weyl operators contribute substantially to biharmonic hypersurfaces being minimal within the Euclidean space.

A rational number p/q represents the basis for a numbering system. Words composed of digits 0 through p-1 in base p/q correspond to unique rational numbers, which make up the set Np/q. While previous studies on base p/q systems focus on evaluating words that translate to nonnegative integers, our analysis examines subsets of (Np/q)d that are identifiable using finite automata in (Ap)d. Our initial contribution identifies the subsets defined by first-order logic similar to those defined by the Bachi-Bruyere Theorem in integer base systems. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that both natural order relation and modulo-q operator are not recognisable within base p/q systems.

Adding three right-handed neutrinos and a simple QCD axion sector to the Standard Model effectively explains multiple phenomena including neutrino oscillations, dark matter, and baryon asymmetry. In doing so, it also resolves issues with strong CP problems and stabilizes the electroweak vacuum while fitting within observational limits of Higgs inflation. The model, referred to as $a\nu$MSM, undergoes a detailed analysis to examine the nature of dark matter within this framework. The presence of an inflection point within Higgs inflation is found not to significantly impact dark matter composition, and thus the model instead presents a multicomponent DM system involving axions along with both light and heavy neutrinos. Through a thermal phase transition triggered by the axion field, massive axions are produced in ample quantities, yet contribute minimally to baryon asymmetry. Meanwhile, DM thermal baths undergo decoupling at different times due to the interaction of gauge forces and the axion field, resulting in the thermal relic density of only the three active-sterile neutrinos being insufficient to satisfy the Planck DM density constraints. Through a variation of the axion decay constant, the model effectively sheds light on the anticipated future updates to DM parameter space as data becomes more precise.

Between October 2019 and April 2020, the LAMOST performed a unique observational study using four $K$2 plates. This study, which involved low- and medium-resolution spectroscopic surveys, gathered a significant amount of data. The low-resolution spectroscopic survey yielded around 767,000 spectra after 25 nights of 46.6 hours of exposures and a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 for about 70% of its spectra. The medium-resolution spectroscopic survey took 177 exposures and around 49.1 hours over 27 nights to collect around 478,000 spectra. The data showed a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 for about 50% of its spectra. To estimate the stellar parameters and radial velocities, the LAMOST research team utilized several different methods such as LASP, DD-Payne, and SLAM. These estimations demonstrated good agreement and were consistent with those of the APOGEE study. By analyzing the $Gaia$ DR2 data, the LAMOST research team corrected for radial velocity zero points on a per exposure basis, showing good alignment with the APOGEE study. Correction of the stellar parameters and radial velocities resulted in significantly reduced total dispersion in the mass estimation of main sequence stars when compared to theoretical expectations. In image recognition, distinct forms of visual cues, namely edges and textures, contribute uniquely to the overall understanding. While edges convey crucial information about a shape's form, textures reveal details about regional appearance. Current Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) applications often excel at extracting texture information but tend to produce vague boundary definitions. Training-based bias can develop during learning, frequently favoring either edge or texture analysis. Our research aims to leverage the strength of both types of information through a novel edge-aware CNN framework, EdNet, which is transferable across various medical image segmentation tasks. EdNet structure is primarily composed of a main network focused on texture extraction within a 3D space and an edge-guided network that derives boundary information from 2D slices, which can be transferable across different imaging modalities. The two networks work in unison to provide input to the main network and directly to the volume binary mask through identity connections, effectively training both network components simultaneously. Experimental evaluations using diverse medical datasets demonstrate that EdNet achieves superior performance, achieving precise boundary definitions and significant improvements over baseline CNN models and state-of-the-art methods, particularly in cases with unclear tissue boundaries.

MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for three different types of transactions: standalone, replica set, and sharded cluster deployments. Considering the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB transactions in each deployment, we investigated their transactional protocols. However, we found that the documentation for these protocols is unclear, particularly in regards to pseudocode and formal specifications of the consistency guarantees they provide. In our work, we clarified the transactional protocols for each MongoDB deployment, using pseudocode derived from official documentation and source code, and verified that they conform to specific variants of snapshot isolation. Our approach also enables efficient checking of the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB's transaction protocols.

Using the elementary symmetric function basis, we re-express the chromatic symmetric functions of Dyck paths with a bounce number of three via a combinatorial interpretation related to the inverse of the Kostka matrix from Egecioglu-Remmel (1990). This analysis shows the positivity of specific coefficients and confirms $e$-positivity for an expanded class of these functions, beyond a particular instance explored in Cho-Huh (2019).

We begin by defining a task for few-shot continual learning and propose a theory to explain how executive function works through a self-updating decision-making system that reprocesses perception data through a review of past experiences in order to minimize prediction errors. This idea becomes practical due to the incorporation of a memory mechanism and a pre-trained neural network that is predisposed to follow rules of effective learning and adapts to optimize its chances of long-term success. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our model of executive function can facilitate the development of hypothesis testing as an internal reasoning process and might provide insight into observed abilities of human learning and the organization of the human brain.

The success of medical image analysis using machine learning largely relies on high-quality datasets.  However, when these datasets contain biases, the models can learn them, compromising their ability to generalize and produce reliable results.  While research exists on developing unbiased models, the problem lies in identifying and mitigating the inherent biases present in medical image datasets.  In an effort to address this issue, we first establish a metric to quantify data intrinsic bias and propose a new framework for detecting biases in medical image datasets.  Our proposed framework, comprising of two primary components, namely KlotskiNet and Bias Discriminant Direction Analysis, aims to identify and quantify the inherent biases present in medical image datasets.  Our experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework in accurately identifying biases.

Research on intricate systems from the human brain to social connections has uncovered a higher-level structure that can be characterized through aggregates of interconnected triangles. To uncover these concealed geometric patterns, we analyze the topological organization of networks through the use of dimer- and triangle-based interactions, represented by the Ising spin system. Our study reveals that sorting spins by reversing their orientation can unveil hidden triangular structures within the network, simultaneously achieving a maximization of a specific entropic measure. Further investigation shows that the application of an external influence in reversing this structural organization follows first-order phase transition patterns. Moreover, analysis of the energy and entropy landscape uncovers multiple stable aggregated configurations, each corresponding to distinct triangle-based structures. The shape of this landscape can be altered by adjusting the weight of triangular interactions and simulating noise-induced hysteresis patterns. These findings provide a theoretical framework for navigating and influencing the hidden geometry of complex networks.

We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we recorded data for 12-day periods right around each encounter. These observations took place as close as 27.8 times the radius of the sun from the solar center, and we based our energy flux calculations on readings for electron density, temperature, and speed, along with the bulk characteristics of solar protons. Combining the data from the four approaches, we found the average energy flux that could reach the solar surface and counteract gravity is about 70 Watts per square meter, plus or minus 14 Watts. Notably, this is similar to the findings of other researchers using data from different spacecraft and covering a longer time period, but with a key difference being that the solar wind energy distributions were much more symmetrical and normally distributed than seen closer to the Earth, likely due to the influence of solar plasma fluctuations being limited by the close distance.

Thanks to speech-emotion recognition technology, computers can engage with people on a more emotional level. Nonetheless, the accuracy of speech-emotion recognition in real-world situations remains an area of improvement. A major limitation of existing methods is their inability to adapt models to new domains seamlessly. In response, researchers have developed innovative domain adaptation techniques that transfer knowledge across domains, yielding significant improvements. While these advancements are promising, there is still room for growth in adapting models to real-time, live data scenarios. A deep reinforcement learning-based strategy is presented here to adapt a pre-trained model in real-time while interacting with its environment. In evaluating the proposed approach on speech-emotion recognition tasks, substantial gains in accuracy are observed compared to baseline methods. Notably, the accuracy improves from around 40% to over 50% in a challenging run on the IAM dataset.

We present an investigation of Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ (BFTO), a four-layer Aurivillius compound, under the influence of high hydrostatic pressure.  Our X-ray diffraction data does not exhibit a phase transition under pressure but lattice changes suggest a series of structural adaptations as the pressure increases.  Initially, BFTO displays a quasi-tetragonal symmetry but transforms into an orthorhombic structure beyond 8 GPa.  Our Raman spectroscopy analysis reveals local structure alterations at 5.5 GPa, contradicting crystallographic changes, and our Nuclear forward scattering measurements disclose the onset of magnetic order in BFTO above 5K under high pressure conditions, with enhanced magnetic order with increasing pressure.  Conversely, NFS at 6.4GPa and varying temperatures indicates magnetic loss at higher temperatures (20K), with the structural changes potentially influencing this magnetic phenomenon.

Hybrid methods tackling continuous shortest path problems start by local optimization
of discrete shortest paths in spatial networks. The convergence to optimal solutions
depends on the discretization error caused by restricting the global search to a network,
with specific implications on the choice of network density. A notable application
is flight planning, which involves determining optimal routes considering factors such
as flight time, fuel consumption, and weather conditions. Advanced algorithms for
discrete shortest paths can be used to compute starting points for locally convergent
methods in optimal control. We establish a priori and localized bounds for the
error in estimated flight times compared to optimal continuous trajectories, taking
into account network density and wind field. These bounds facilitate designing
networks with optimal connectivity, and the derived bounds are illustrated through
benchmarks, which show significant improvements in localization but still offer scope
for refinement through additional estimators.

Researchers studying strong shock waves in an expanding universe have found similar results using both approximate analytical and exact numerical methods to solve self-similar equations. When the adiabatic index lies between one and approximately 1.16, these solutions consistently occupy all space without gaps, showing close alignment with each other. As the index surpasses this threshold, pressure drops to zero at a finite distance from the origin, and in both scenarios, a spherical void forms. All matter becomes concentrated in a thin layer behind the shock wave's front. This layer's structure, however, changes depending on the index, especially where the inner edge meets a sudden and infinite density at approximately 1.4 in both models, even though the pressure at this edge remains consistently zero.

Using 13 TeV proton-proton collision data, specifically 1.7 inverse femtobarns of luminosity collected by the LHCb detector, the shape of the $B_s^0\rightarrow D_s^{*-}\mu^+\nu_{\mu}$ differential decay rate is determined as a function of hadron recoil. This rate is reconstructed via the $D_s^{-}$ decay sequence into $K^-K^+\pi^-$, following $D_s^{*-}$ decay into $D_s^{-}\gamma$, with the photon being undetected. The analysis considers final state phase space dynamics and theoretical predictions from倩cut-off effective field theory, while extracting form factor values from a global analysis by the HFLAV collaboration. Template shapes for the decay rate are formed using simulated samples and compared between simulations and actual measurements of the $D_s^{-}$ momentum spectrum. The rate for right-handed $W-$boson coupling is independently derived from data and found to match standard model expectations at 0.15 statistical and 0.04 systematic precision.

A recent paper provides an analysis of advancements made in categorizing monodromy-free Schrödinger operators with rational potential properties. A specific subset of potential properties is studied which comprise generalized Hermite polynomials, constructed through the use of Wronskians from standard Hermite polynomials, often seen in mathematical physics and random matrix theories. This class of quadratic potentials displays oscillatory behavior near the origin and our study identifies the precise condition under which potentials remain non-singular, resulting in a discrete set of parameters. For each parameter, asymptotic polynomial solutions are derived which align with standard Hermite polynomials at certain energy levels. Furthermore, one can establish a connection between generalized Hermite polynomials and the monodromy-free Schrödinger operator, thereby revealing their physical significance. Additionally, our approach facilitates transformation of standardized harmonic oscillators into systems governed by these generalized Hermite polynomials through the use of factorization techniques.

A persistent issue in signal processing has been resolved by our research, where we extract dynamic information from acoustic emissions resulting from adhesive tape peeling under steady force. Through phase space reconstruction, our findings reveal the deterministic chaotic nature of these dynamics by confirming the existence of a correlation dimension and a positive Lyapunov exponent at specific traction velocities. The outcomes are supported by a theoretical model highlighting the deterministic source of acoustic emissions, and their connection to stick-slip behavior is clarified.

In epitaxial InAs/Al structures, our experimental analysis reveals the stochastic behavior of planar Josephson junctions and SQUIDs as temperature varies, exhibiting a crossover between macroscopic quantum tunneling and phase diffusion. The threshold temperature for this phase transition, T*, is directly related to the zero-temperature critical current I_c(0) through a universal relationship, with only material and geometric factors determining the proportionality. This discovered universal vicinity allows for the general application of measurements taken in different ranges around T*. Furthermore, when the thermal energy surpasses the critical energy, thermal fluctuations lead to an exponential reduction of I_c due to bias, with thermal activation rates providing insights into thermal phase slip barriers across various energy scales. Our study also highlights thermal activation in a weak junction as a potential model system for thermal superconducting phase diffusion, with activation rates indicating dynamic thermal equilibrium.

The Yang-Mills-aether theory is analyzed to understand the implications of introducing non-abelian aether-like terms that violate Lorentz symmetry, specifically within thermal quantum field theory. By incorporating temperature effects and spatial compactification via Thermofield Dynamics, corrections to the non-abelian Stefan-Boltzmann law and non-abelian Casimir energy and pressure are calculated for both zero and finite temperatures.

This research develops a method for estimating the expected cost of hedging European options through the delta-hedging process, resulting in a computationally efficient formula that accounts for option prices and the behavior of delta processes. Initially, a standard unit hedging cost is established and subsequently, the total hedging cost is determined as the product of this unit cost, stock price, a supply curve factor, and the square of the number of options. Consequently, this formulation enables faster computation of expected hedging costs than alternative Monte Carlo methods. The study also provides explicit numerical examples demonstrating the practical applications of this method in specific contexts.

By applying variational techniques, we develop a limiting model for a set of functionals subject to linear differential constraints. This framework models the energy of a heterogeneous material with a high-contrast composite structure at a microscopic scale, comprising a periodically perforated matrix filled with a dissimilar substance. Our key finding involves analyzing the $\Gamma$-convergence as the material periodicity diminishes, demonstrating that the limit functional comprises two components: the stored energy within the matrix, and the stored energy within the fillings. To overcome the coercivity issue inherent in the material structure, we employ two-scale convergence methods, while novel results are established for addressing the linear differential constraints via existence proofs for potentials and constraint-preserving extension operators.

We undertook a statistical investigation into tidal features surrounding early-type galaxies of massive proportions, utilizing data from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program. Our analysis revealed that roughly 28 percent of 2649 galaxies, selected due to their mass greater than $10^{11}M_{\odot}$ and within a redshift range of 0.05-0.15, exhibited distinct tidal features exceeding one percent flux fraction. Observations indicated an exponential decline in the number of galaxies as tidal features became more pronounced. Additionally, within our defined stellar mass scope, we observed tidal features increase in frequency as stellar masses did. To explore the cause of tidal features and tidal features within a cosmic scale, we calculated the radio frequency occurrence rate derived from HSC and radio data from the Square Kilometre Array Pathfinder. No correlation was found between tidal features and radio residual, suggesting that tidal features cannot be explained solely by major mergers. Instead, we estimate the minimum rate of major mergers with ratio greater than four percent per decade in log mass, consistent with recent studies.

A higher education system or similar opportunities can drive social mobility across generations by allowing individuals to rise above their family's economic status. To examine this dynamic in societies with social mobility limitations, a new model allocates opportunities to maximize the benefits they provide to current and future generations. Our model reveals that, in order to maximize long-term payoffs, it's beneficial to give priority to lower socioeconomically situated individuals who have greater potential to rise to better socioeconomical standings. The result can lead to socioeconomic affirmative action. The duration and intensity of this practice vary depending on specific conditions. The proposed model also offers avenues for exploring more intricate relationships between different socioeconomical groups in various societal settings.

The combination of chirped pulse amplification and nonlinear optical systems has been the foundation for significant progress in numerous sectors, including semiconductors, communications, biology, defense, and national security. Understanding the intricate dynamics of these complex laser systems, comprised of multiple coupled components, is crucial for maximizing their potential in generating highly powerful, stable lasers. Our innovative measurement technique successfully deciphers the comprehensive temporal and spectral characteristics of these ultra-brief laser pulses across a wide power scale. In this study, we present successful examples of designing, optimizing, and reverse-engineering both CPA-based and SO-based laser systems utilizing our method. Notably, our achievement successfully captured the complex pulse characteristics of a 200-TW CPA system and a 500-W SO system.

It is proven that for each $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$ and $x_1,\ldots,x_n \in L_p(\mu)$ where the largest absolute value among them does not exceed $K$, there exist vectors $y_1,\ldots,y_n \in \ell_p^d$ such that the dimension $d$ is less than or equal to $\frac{32e^2 (2K)^{2p}\log n}{\varepsilon^2}$, and for all $i, j \in \{1,\ldots,n\}$, the inequality $ \|x_i - x_j\|^p_{L_p(\mu)} - \varepsilon \leq \|y_i - y_j\|_{\ell_p^d}^p \leq \|x_i - x_j\|^p_{L_p(\mu)} + \varepsilon$ holds. Additionally, an algorithm which computes $\{y_i\}_{i=1}^n$ after taking $\{x_i\}_{i=1}^n$ as input exists and relies on techniques from empirical method and combinatorial theory along with $L_p(\mu)$ factorization theory. In 2015, CERN introduced "Emittance Scans," a new fast luminosity separation scanning method at the Large Hadron Collider. These scans were consistently carried out during physics production runs, utilizing full-intensity beams at the CMS experiment's interaction point. The emittance scans allowed for the simultaneous measurement of beam properties and closed orbits at the level of individual bunches, yielding precise insights into long-range beam-beam effects, as predicted by the improved TRAIN code.

This paper explores the optimization challenges in multi-agent systems that involve agents behaving maliciously, which leads to a misdirection away from optimal solutions through the spread of false information and significant communication costs. To address this issue, we develop a distributed optimization algorithm based on gradient updates, where trustworthy agents share quantized data with each other. Theoretical proof of solution convergence near the optimal solution is provided, along with the effects of communication constraints and malicious behavior on solution accuracy. This is further illustrated through numerical experiments presented in the study.

The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a fundamental tool in physical cosmology research. However, the signal's weakness necessitates sophisticated and highly sensitive experiments that observe the sky across various frequencies with thousands of polarisation-sensitive detectors. As such experiments become increasingly sensitive, they are susceptible to being limited by instrumental systematic effects when trying to fully utilise their data. This paper presents a Python tool,'s4cmb', which generates simulated raw data streams in the time domain for contemporary cosmic microwave background experiments based on bolometric technology. The package also incorporates realistic instrumental systematic effects into the simulated data, with the goal of helping researchers assess the impact of such effects on actual data, informing future instrument design, and making simulated data sets more realistic for the development of accurate data analysis techniques.

In the task of arranging unordered words into a meaningful order, prior approaches rely on either linear models or neural networks, without examining the role of pre-trained language models, including why they would be beneficial. Utilizing BART as an example, we find it to be a suitable model for this task and explore its capabilities by conducting additional analysis using probing, which reveals that the syntactic dependencies inherent to BART significantly contribute to its performance. Furthermore, we discover improvements in using BART in a related task known as partial tree linearization.

The rapid dissemination of ultra-realistic media over social platforms necessitates the immediate development of an efficient and adaptable technique for identifying deepfakes. Deepfake creation methods inadvertently leave distinguishing patterns in the frequency spectra of fabricated images and videos. Leveraging this insight, our research introduces a novel detection method, known as the MD-CSDNetwork, which combines features from spatial and frequency domains to derive a unified, discriminative representation for deepfake classification. The proposed network architecture, comprising two parallel branches processing spatial and frequency information, is designed to treat multiple domain inputs as interconnected learning signals. Through cross-stitch connections between the branches, our system automatically identifies an optimal blend of domain-specific and shared features, thereby enhancing performance and generalization. Evaluations conducted on the widely-used FaceForeniscs++ benchmark demonstrate improved classification results for various manipulation types and comparable performance to state-of-the-art approaches on the Celeb-DF and Deepfake Detection Dataset.

Current studies examining the performance of randomly assembled low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes usually assume the independence of degree distributions from edge endpoints. In contrast, our research extends this understanding by investigating LDPC ensembles that incorporate degree-degree correlations. We propose novel techniques for generating degree-degree correlated LDPC ensembles, derive density evolution equations applicable to binary erasure channels, and employ numerical simulations to illustrate how degree-degree correlations impact LDPC code performance. Interestingly, our findings indicate that negative degree-degree correlations can enhance the maximum error tolerance of LDPC codes, with further increases potentially yielding superior unequal error protection designs.

A critical flaw exists in the current application of quantum key distribution (QKD) systems due to their vulnerability to quantum hacking. Our novel approach incorporates a hybrid measurement attack, achievable with only basic components such as linear optics, homodyne detection, and single photon detection, which poses a significant threat to the widely adopted vacuum+weak decoy state QKD system. Specifically, if the source phase is randomly altered to a limited degree, we discovered that the proposed attack can bypass the system's security, resulting in the entanglement-breaking channel without being detected by the users. Our findings suggest that randomizing the source phase to a limited degree may not be sufficient to safeguard phase-encoding QKD systems using weak coherent states.

To effectively manage the vast amounts of data being generated by a growing number of mobile and IoT devices, future mobile networks (MNs) must shift from traditional resource allocation methods. By integrating computation capabilities into Base Stations, we can optimize resource usage and efficiently manage resources near the edge of the network. Leveraging techniques such as time-series forecasting and control theory, we propose using neural networks and optimizing strategies within the Multi-access Edge Computing paradigm. Our approach involves online algorithms for virtualized resource scaling, reconfiguring computing and communication assets, and enabling dynamic BS switching to minimize energy consumption and ensure Quality of Service (QoS). Numerical results demonstrate that these strategies lead to significant reductions in edge computing and communication energy consumption, promoting energy self-sustainability in MNs through the use of green energy sources.

In 1930, mathematician K. Menger developed an interest in the abstract concept of angle function, which he then generalized for use in metric and semi-metric spaces. Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the existence of spaces with certain angular properties. This note aims to provide a space with these properties as well as two examples of spaces that cannot accommodate certain dimensional capacities. These latter examples, which cannot support a specific function property in dimensions three and higher, were first described by J. Tits in 1964 but within a different context.

Consider a number field $K$ of degree $n \geq 2$, embedded in the complex plane $\mathbb{C}$, and define its norm as the geometric mean of the squared absolute values of its $n$ embeddings. For any order $\mathcal{O}$ in $K$, the successive minima $\lambda_0 = 1 \leq \dots \leq \lambda_{n-1}$ with respect to this norm determine the inequality structure. Inspired by Lenstra's conjecture, we seek to characterize all inequalities of the form $1 \ll_{\mathcal{S}} \lambda_1^{f_1}\dots\lambda_{n-1}^{f_{n-1}}$, for an infinite set $\mathcal{S}$ of isomorphism classes of orders, for various sets $\mathcal{S}$, especially those based on field or subfield properties. For degrees $n$ with certain prime factorization properties (such as being prime powers or products of two primes), we establish a combinatorial classification of the integers defining relationships between minima and provide analogues of our results for ideals in number fields and curves, examining the interplay between minima and other geometric invariants.

We utilize 1-d fs/ps hybrid rotational coherent anti-Stokes Raman spectroscopy with dual probes to make comprehensive measurements of gas temperature, pressure, and oxygen-to-nitrogen ratios. By harnessing the power of time and frequency-domain measurements, a cutting-edge technique offers unprecedented accuracy (<1%) and precision (0.42%) for determining pressure. Initially demonstrated in a sealed environment over a pressure range (1-1.5 bar), the method effectively captures intricate pressure variations resulting from nitrous gas interacting with a solid surface in various states of flow. Notably, it can also detect very fine-scale pressure differences arising from the conversion of kinetic energy into pressure as well as distinct O2/N2 patterns formed by turbulent mixing processes.

The traditional theory of planetary formation through core accretion has limitations when explaining how small particles overcome early development obstacles in a protoplanetary disk. A more recent model proposes the viscous ring-instability to account for ring structures in protoplanetary disks. It suggests that particles may reduce the disk's conductivity, inhibiting the growth of instability. Using GPU-based simulations of interacting gas and dust, this study investigates this model's validity. As the disk evolves, ring structures become unstable, breaking into smaller whirlpools, and subsequently forming stable dust formations. These structures provide a conducive environment for the growth of planetary building blocks through gravitational collapse. Small viscosity values lead to larger and more stable ring structures, while higher values result in more complex patterns. The nested instability model can generate a wide range of observed structures in protoplanetary disks and creates ideal conditions for planetary system formation.

Quantum Hall phases exhibit gapped behavior in the interior while supporting both chiral and neutral edge modes.  A specific setup involving a path that only includes neutral modes, essential for an electric current from the source to the drain, is examined here. When a source is biased in this circuit, it is observed that an electric current can be measured at the drain, provided that backscattering between opposing modes at the contact locations is present. The result shows that neutral modes hold relevant information and can be used for a nonlocal reconstruction of a dc charge current. The described protocol may be employed to detect any neutral mode that counter-propagates with respect to charge modes, and this detection approach is applicable not only to the edge modes of quantum Hall systems but also to systems possessing neutral modes that do not originate from quantum Hall effects. Finally, an experimental demonstration of this concept is proposed.

We introduce a rigid cluster model to represent the quantum group U_q(g), with Lie algebra U_q(g) being of simply laced type, A-D-E. For U_q(g), we establish a non-degenerate map to a quantum cluster algebra C_q(W), with winding group W being of the same Lie algebra U_q(g). The algebra C_q(W) is defined by quantum cluster variables and S- and T- transformations being quantum cluster automorphisms. Notably, the quantum cluster algebra C_q(W) possesses a natural C*-completion C*(W), with its elements having well-defined representations. We demonstrate that U_q(g) is isomorphic to a subalgebra of C*(W).

In our research paper, we address the distributionally robust decentralized learning problem by adapting the robust distribution to a decentralized context. We introduce an effective algorithm that integrates the concepts of robust optimization and average consensus to achieve this. Our method involves each participant adjusting their local model to the most adverse shifted data and then sharing this with neighbors through an average consensus process. We prove that DR-DSGD converges to an optimal solution within a finite number of iterations, establishing a direct relationship between the number of iterations and both the curvature and condition of the graph. Additionally, DR-DSGD has broader applications, such as enhancing federated and edge learning systems by guarding against malicious data and biased aggregation tendencies. Finally, our findings are supported by numerical experiments.

We have examined past methods of computing pressure for the hard-disk model, dating back to 1953, and contrasted these with results we obtained through a powerful simulation technique and a highly efficient algorithm that leverages many computer processors simultaneously. Like various simple scientific models, such as the Drosophila model, understanding the hard-disk model required significant effort. In our research, we argue that the difficulty of this understanding stems from an insufficient exploration of phase-space in existing computer simulations, particularly as they approach and move away from high-density transitions. Our comparative analysis with a simulation technique that samples a vast portion of phase-space in two dimensions reveals a distinct movement pattern, suggesting that the difficulty of the hard-disk model may be attributed to a limitation of computer processing power rather than the nature of the model itself. Furthermore, our efficiency gains over previous records with three, two, and one-dimensional equations of state are attributed to this technique combined with targeted simulations using clusters of computer processors, suggesting that future breakthroughs in understanding complex systems may arise from advancements in computing technology rather than developments in simulation algorithms.

This paper examines jet modifications within a medium using JEWEL and PYTHIA 6.4, emphasizing uncertainties associated with perturbative scales, nuclear PDFs, and temperature variations of the medium at onset and transition points. Jet spectrum and nuclear modification factor data from the LHC are used for comparison with simulated results. Additionally, the influence of nuclear PDFs and the medium on jet structure is investigated through Lund plane analysis, and the interaction between nuclear PDF choice and medium parameters is explored.

Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with unprecedented visibility of its transactions. By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible code and transaction records, our study explores the intricate workings of the scheme, its impact on users, and its evolution. Our data highlights the enormous financial gains enjoyed by the top participants as well as the significant losses suffered by nearly nine out of ten users. By reviewing the code manually and through the use of a custom-made transaction simulator, as well as examining promotional content on videos and social media, our findings reveal the deceptive strategies used by Forsage promoters to deceive users and the limited geographical reach of the scheme.

The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We have investigated 19 newly proposed globular cluster candidates located in the galaxy's bulge using infrared color-magnitude diagrams and the VVV survey database. We computed key astrophysical properties including the reduction of light passing through interstellar gas, distance from Earth, total brightness, average cluster movement through space, metal composition, and age. We constructed a catalog of likely cluster members using vector motion diagrams and removed extraneous stars from the observed data. We compared the theoretical relationships between physical properties and their observational equivalents for a sample of proven cluster members with external field stars. We discovered that eight of the proposed candidates are actually existing globular clusters, while the remaining ten are either small open clusters, dense areas surrounded by stellar nuclei, or false positives consisting of multiple clusters superimposed on each other and not visible in optical wavelengths. We have highlighted the importance of verifying proposed globular cluster candidates with optical surveys before considering them confirmed.

A set of precise theoretical and experimental benchmarks at hadron colliders are based on color-singlet differential spectra, known as exclusive differential spectra. Our study provides a comprehensive effective-theory framework, using soft-collinear effective theory to account for heavy-quark effects in differential distributions at various scale hierarchies, specifically considering the splitting of gluons into heavy-quark pairs alongside the primary contributions of heavy-quarks in hard-scattering processes. This particular research centers around the Drell-Yan process and focuses on vector-boson transverse momentum, $q_T$, and beam thrust, $\mathcal T$, to illustrate exclusive observables that are measurable in collider experiments, employing proton-proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider as case studies to demonstrate tree-level factorization theorems for $q_T$ and $\mathcal T$. Additionally, it presents NNLO matching for heavy-quark contributions in the dominant scale hierarchy of $\{Q, \Lambda_{\rm QCD}, q_T\}$, along with numerical assessments to examine the impact of perturbative quark and heavy-quark contributions, particularly in regions of interest for LHC measurements.

We examine the techniques of simulating light-matter interactions within tight-binding models that derive from first-principle theory. The conventional method for describing optical properties uses a velocity-based approach tied to the vector potential. An alternative method exists, where a finite system is represented through the electric field, resulting in a dipole-based model inspired by Peierls substitution. This study evaluates the accuracy of both methods in relation to gauge invariance, utilizing TB models constructed from maximally localized Wannier functions and applied to two-dimensional paradigm materials. We calculate the electromagnetic responses under linear and strong excitations, comparing the outcomes to converged first-principle simulations to validate our TB models' accuracy. The results indicate that the dipole-based model yields a more precise description than the velocity-based model. We attribute this to the imperfect compensation of diamagnetic and paramagnetic currents in the velocity-based model. To rectify this shortcoming, we formulated a sum rule that explicitly addresses the compensation issue, allowing the correction of velocity-based models to match dipole-based models and guarantee gauge invariance.

In this context, we explore certain classes of holographic tensor networks, which can efficiently simulate various systems using the principle of minimization, serve as quantum codes to prevent information loss, and accurately describe phenomena exhibiting power-law behaviors. A key finding reveals that networks comprising a single type of tensor and possessing erasure correction capabilities can't simultaneously possess certain desirable traits - those that facilitate the efficient calculation of physical properties through a local process and those necessary for an accurate representation of power-law behaviors in data. This contradiction motivates the creation of network guidelines that utilize diverse types of tensors, allowing these networks to successfully capture the characteristics of power-law behaviors while adhering to the principle of efficient calculation. A concrete example of such a network has also been developed - one that closely resembles the holographic HaPPY pentagon code under the assumption that specific system parameters can be set to a particular small range.

A theoretical analysis of retinal chromophore photoisomerization in rhodopsin utilized a model incorporating thermal baths and dual states. It was observed that quantum yields in a steady-state condition (occurring 10 ps after the reaction begins and onwards) differ notably from their short-lived counterparts, indicating an imperfect correlation between transient and sustained behaviors. Furthermore, the steady-state quantum yield was shown to be exquisitely sensitive to minor adjustments in system parameters, in stark contrast to the relative insensitivity of transient dynamics. Analysis of this sensitivity in relation to nonadiabatic vibronic level spacing suggests that quantum chaos might underlie this phenomenon, and potential avenues for experimental validation along with implications in complex light-sensitive systems are explored.

Deep-learning techniques such as Convolutional Neural Networks and Recurrent
Neural Networks have seen significant success in process-mining applications.
Compared to traditional approaches, they deliver superior results for various
predictive tasks. Our research expands on existing knowledge by testing five
different variants of deep learning models, including Graph Neural Networks and
Multi-layer Perceptron with dropout, for predicting the characteristics and
occurrence time of subsequent process events. Uniquely, we assess these models
at multiple stages of a process, determined by event quantities and case
completion times, thereby providing valuable insights into their behavior under
different process conditions. Our experiments surprisingly reveal that the basic
Multi-layer Perceptron frequently surpasses more advanced deep learning models
in both prediction tasks. Consequently, when deploying predictive process models,
due caution is required as they perform differently across various process stages
and it's essential to avoid excessive reliance on sophisticated deep learning
models.

Turkey is prone to seismic activities with varying intensity earthquakes occurring frequently, emphasizing the necessity for swift and effective crisis information dissemination. Social media can provide valuable insights into public perception, beneficial for crisis communication and management. This research focuses on analyzing Twitter posts related to the 2020 Izmir earthquake, aiming to leverage these insights to infer real-time public opinions. By combining data mining techniques with natural language processing, we examine public sentiment and topic discussions following the earthquake. Our approach utilized LDA for topic modeling and BERT for sentiment analysis. Results show users shared supportive messages and engaged with relief efforts, expressing their desire to have their concerns heard by authorities. The implemented methodology demonstrated success, and future directions for related studies are also outlined.

We investigate key properties of several types of Gelfand-Shilov spaces, which are characterized by the decay of their smooth functions and their Fourier transforms. The nontriviality of these spaces, specifically ${\Sigma}^{\sigma}_s$, is shown to depend on the values of $s$ and ${\sigma}$ being greater than 1. The text further presents growth estimates for functions within one-parameter spaces, and it also establishes relationships between short-time Fourier transforms and these spaces. Moreover, conditions are established to ensure that Toeplitz operators are continuous when applied to functions within one-parameter spaces.

Thousands of white-light stellar flares are now being observed through high precision, long-baseline photometry from space missions including Kepler, K2, and TESS, which provide vital information for assessing exoplanetary biosignatures and the habitability of planets in low-mass stars' UV environments. Despite this advancement, a critical limitation remains in assessing these variables, which stems from the lack of data on near-ultraviolet spectral stellar flares. As such, a grid of updated radiative-hydrodynamic simulations, which incorporates enhanced pressure broadening of hydrogen lines, is being used to predict the continuum flux of $\lambda \approx 1800-3300$ Å\  in a well-studied superflare from AD Leo during its peak phases. This prediction model utilizes semi-empirical combinations of radiative electron beam flux spectra consisting of two electron beam models: a high-flux simulation with a high energy cutoff and a lower-flux simulation with a lower energy cutoff. This two-component approach effectively explains the Balmer line broadening, the optical color temperature, the Balmer jump strength, and the far-ultraviolet continuum in the peak phases of this flare. Additionally, a comparative analysis is conducted with solar flare data, including those from the Interface Region Imaging Spectrograph, which provide spatial resolution, combined with previous modeling of the SOL20140329T17:48 X1 solar flare, to demonstrate that the two

This investigation into the PT-symmetric waveguide network's behavior uses mathematical models to derive exact equations describing wave propagation in a finite number of connected units. Analyzing this through generalized parametric space, researchers discovered that when PT symmetry breaks, propagating modes appear consistently, unaffected by the unit cell's transmission phase or number. However, at PT-symmetric equilibrium, mode formation relies on the transmission phase. Notably, for specific PT-symmetric states in unit cells lacking general mode formation, adding one more unit cell can restore mode creation. Experimental verification was achieved using acoustic wave propagation in a two-unit cell network, demonstrating exceptional dual functionality in a PT-symmetric network with equal numbers of gain and loss components. Lastly, theoretical analysis showed that a PT-symmetric laser can emerge from a coherent absorption process in this network.

We study the behavior and evolution of Boolean networks with sparse connections that interact with themselves using Glauber dynamics, where the dynamics occurs simultaneously for all elements in the network. Equilibrium is evaluated by rapidly flipping the input for each unit and assessing the influence of other units on the system. 

Furthermore, we introduce an efficient technique to measure how one unit affects another during the evolution, called Transfer Operator Dynamics (TOD), which involves comparing the systems with and without the source unit forcing the target unit to a specific state. Our method allows for the calculation of TOD matrices that can reveal the long-term and dynamic relationships between units, and there is a theoretical confirmation that the TOD matrices accurately reflect the equilibrium state through a connection to the Transfer Operator State Space Reconstruction (TOSSR) theorem. 

We implement TOD and TOSSR using efficient simulations that allow us to investigate the equilibrium and dynamic behavior of Boolean networks with sparse interactions, including complex systems modeling earthquakes, and our method even provides accurate results for systems exhibiting metastability.

We derive concise mathematical expressions for calculating matrix elements of single-particle and particle-particle operators that can be applied to a wide range of Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov wave functions, encompassing configurations involving multiple quasiparticle excitations. Furthermore, our test simulations demonstrate the significant potential of these formulas to streamline the restoration of symmetry within large and complex nuclear systems.

Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them. Neural networks can be made more robust through weight adjustments but this makes models difficult to interpret and slows their performance. An alternative approach of adding a smoothing layer prior to input processing has been shown effective in enhancing accuracy. However, this approach's inability to generalize to unaltered data and complicated implementation limits its application in neural network points cloud models. In an effort to address these limitations, we present the Transformation Specific Smoothing (TSS) layer which focuses on enhancing clarity following shape transformations, can be applied to arbitrary data, and offers easy integration with existing models. Our results demonstrate that TSS significantly boosts accuracy and clarity across various types of unaltered data and provides superior performance to other smoothing techniques in neural network points cloud models.

We're investigating medium access techniques in Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar networks with all radar units utilizing identical settings, such as sweep duration and frequency characteristics. We're developing and evaluating performance metrics for two medium access methods: ALOHA in time slices and carrier sense multiple access. Specifically, we created a theoretical model for packet transmission success rates in time slice ALOHA and conducted computer simulations to validate this model. We also analyzed the network's efficiency with this protocol. Furthermore, we introduced a new variant of time slice ALOHA, where users wait for open channels and discovered its theoretical and simulated packet transmission success rates. We also developed a novel analytical model for CSMA, introducing the concept of virtual packet size and comparing its efficiency to time slice ALOHA. Our findings indicate that a form of ALOHA, specifically the 'wait-for-open-sweep' variant, outperforms traditional time slice ALOHA, and that our virtual packet size-based CSMA protocol surpasses even this enhanced ALOHA protocol.

Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a leading approach for
inferring accurate and missing event and temporal knowledge graph information.
Building upon successful applications of tensor decomposition in static graph
completions, we introduce Time-LowFER - an extension of the low-rank factorization
model that is both efficient in parameters and attentive to time constraints.
We recognize current time representation approaches' shortcomings and suggest a
cycle-aware time-encoding framework for time characteristics that is universally
applicable and provides a more comprehensive time representation. Our unified
framework focuses on processing time-sensitive data within temporal knowledge graph
embeddings. Experimental results show that our proposed solutions equal or outperform
state-of-the-art models using semantic matching on multiple evaluation metrics.

Within the RPA framework, the Jost function method has been enhanced to detect the complex eigenenergies of RPA excitations. By applying this method, the complex 16-megaelectronvolt resonance within 16O has been identified within the RPA spectrum, demonstrating that the RPA successfully identifies this resonance resulting from collective $16$O excitation outside the mean-field spectrum. Furthermore, the complex eigenenergy within RBA can be understood through the zero-energy Jost factors derived from the small-amplitude quantum fluctuations about the distorted 16O ground state.

Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages time-series data to detect communities within dynamic systems by defining a state similarity measure that reflects mutual influence and utilizes the Koopman operator to handle nonlinear relationships, thus extending the approach to a broad spectrum of applications. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through clustering of a linear system, the non-linear 39-bus transmission network, and variables derived from atmospheric data in the Amazon rainforest.

Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task because the training process is non-differentiable. Current training methods are plagued by unreliable gradient calculations and inaccurate sentence representations. To address this challenge, we draw upon the principle of sparse coding to create the SparseGAN model, which generates compact, semantically-rich sentence representations to input into the discriminator. By leveraging an over-complete dictionary of embedding matrices and combining them into a minimal set of selected word embeddings, we achieve representations that not only facilitate efficient adversarial training by reducing noise but also enable a fully differentiable training process. Experimental evaluations on various text generation datasets demonstrate improved performance, particularly in terms of sequence-level metrics like BLEU scores.

The idea that life could be transferred from one planetary system to another, a concept known as interstellar panspermia, has its roots in the distant past, but the challenge remains of being able to observe this theory in action. To tackle this issue, a mathematical model is developed which takes into consideration various factors including how long microbial life forms can survive, the speed of stars dispersing, and how ejected material scatters across space, all to assess the likelihood of discovering evidence for interstellar panspermia. By examining statistical relationships between pairs of life-bearing planetary systems, a potential indicator of interstellar panspermia emerges under specific assumptions regarding meteorite integrity and life form resilience. Maps of possible outcomes for these life-forms, termed "survival surfaces," can illustrate the complex balance of these factors, but detecting interstellar panspermia may require observing vast numbers of planetary systems in existence for extended periods.

Using the Effective Field Theory of Large Scale Structure, we make predictions for HI intensity mapping power spectrum multipoles based on perturbation theory. These predictions will allow us to constrain cosmological parameters using moderate-resolution surveys that are expected to be conducted with next-generation radio interferometers. To accurately compare the predicted and observed data, we modify the standard comparison integral to account for the finite resolution of future surveys. On resolution-scaled wavenumbers, the real and velocity space halo models accurately describe the observed data up to $k_\pi \sim 0.3\, h\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$, where they also align with the perturbation theory predictions. The choice of foreground removal method can affect the interpretation of observed data. For instance, when applying a sharp $k$-space filter, velocity dispersion can significantly impact the observed quadrupole even at linear order. Similarly, top-hat filtering can cause the observed hexadecapole to appear even when no hexadecapole signal is actually generated by the method. Furthermore, elliptical $k$-space filtering can utilize hexadecapole information to improve the precision of six scalar cosmological parameter estimation up to $\sim 5\%$ of its optimal achievement.

The proposed concept of induced spontaneous symmetry breaking is explored through a theoretical scenario. This scenario posits that spontaneous symmetry breaking occurs at the highest energy level, causing a cascade of symmetry violations at lower energy levels resulting from subtle mixings between them. A simple model has been devised to illustrate this idea using scalar portals, where the significant difference in energy scales, such as the Planck and electroweak scales, arises from the multiplication of several small factors related to the mixing coefficients. The formation of dark matter is also examined in this framework, where it could emerge from the lowest energy level that experienced spontaneous symmetry breaking, or from the interaction or decay products of heavier particles.

Animal population studies often prioritize understanding how animals utilize space and select resources, which are typically analyzed using telemetry data and resource selection functions.  Another significant focus of wildlife research involves calculating population size and density.  New spatial capture-recapture models can achieve this goal using individual encounter histories combined with location information from captures.  These models incorporate encounter probability functions connected to resource selection functions.  However, no previous studies have explored combining capture-recapture and resource selection data to estimate space usage, resource selection, and population density simultaneously.  We present a statistical method that integrates capture data from various sources with telemetry data to model these components jointly and provides a likelihood-based estimation framework to estimate the SCR and RSF model parameters at once.  This method results in enhanced precision in population density estimates and offers unbiased estimates of population density even when telemetry data do not cover the entire area where animals are being captured.  Compared to analyzing capture and telemetry data separately, our method improves precision of population density estimates by an average of 37%.  We illustrate our approach with a case study on pika estimates in the Sierra Nevada mountains, achieving comparable results to traditional capture-recapture and telemetry methods but with greater precision.  We argue that combining capture and telemetry data is becoming increasingly feasible as telemetry data quality improves and more historical telemetry datasets are made available for analysis.  Our method leverages these datasets to produce more precise space usage, resource selection, and population density estimates.

In designing minimum power networks, we are given an undirected graph $G = (V, E)$ along with associated edge costs. The objective is to select an edge-disjoint set of $st$-paths from $G$, consisting of $k$ paths, that minimize the maximum cost encountered in any single path.

We introduce a novel approximation algorithm for this problem with a ratio of $O(\sqrt{\log |V| \cdot \log k})$. Furthermore, for instances where the graph edges satisfy a specific condition - edge costs adhering to the triangle inequality - our algorithm achieves a ratio of $O(\sqrt{\log |V| \cdot \log k})$. Additionally, we present a variant of this algorithm that attains a ratio of $O(\sqrt{k \log |V| \log k})$ without requiring the triangle inequality condition.

This study proposes a technique for the autonomous planning of swarms of unmanned aerial vehicles within a predefined environment. When the swarm detects changes, such as the movement of a target, within a designated area, the command center recalculates and adjusts the swarm's flight path. Key algorithms employed in this research are A* pathfinding and Generalized Labeled Multi-Bernoulli for target tracking.

The concept of localization in physics is significant in understanding dynamic processes on complex networks, particularly near critical transitions. This study tackles this issue by measuring nodal activity to quantify localization in networks undergoing dynamic changes. The proposed method is widely applicable and can be employed with theoretical models, simulated data, and real-world observations. The researchers analyze spreading processes, determining how node degree and centrality affect localization in a general manner. Theoretically, they demonstrate that dynamic processes exhibit inherent localization patterns, and the proposed measure can predict this behavior. Furthermore, the proposed method reveals that different processes exhibit distinct localization preferences and can identify an implicit organizational structure in networks based on dynamic processes.

Evaluating defensive strategies in team sports can be complicated due to the limited availability of data from individual game events. Previous researchers developed methods for assessing football teams' defensive prowess by predicting the likelihood of gaining possession of the ball and being attacked, based on the location of all players involved. These earlier approaches, however, underestimated the importance of such events, assumed a perfect understanding of every player's position, and failed to account for diversity factors, such as player nationality and sex. To overcome these limitations, we present a revised approach to valuing defensive teams by first predicting the probability of being attacked and gaining possession of the ball, given the location of all players during 40 international men's games at the 2022 UEFA EURO and 40 women's games at the 2022 UEFA EURO. By comparing predicted to actual outcomes, we calculated the generalised valuation of defence (GVD) scores, which showed a clear distinction between winning and losing teams, producing a score of 1.57 on the score-tuple. Additionally, GVD scores demonstrated a negative correlation (r = -0.63, p = 0.01) with final league scores, indicating that this approach effectively captures the value of defensive teams regardless of the direction of play.

Extracting information from images of forms is a complex task due to varying layout designs. This complexity increases with old forms that have deteriorated and are contaminated with noise. One crucial step in the extraction process involves linking input text to predefined label fields. Our research offers an innovative, layout-agnostic method to identify pre-printed text, handwriting, and their relationships. Our technique excels in handling imperfect form images, unlike previous approaches designed for well-organized images. To test its effectiveness, we created a database of deteriorated forms from the late 1800s and early 1900s. Our model uses a neural network to identify both types of text, after which we classify their relationships through the analysis of the detected text features. Our research indicates that our relationship-determination technique performs better than rule-based methods and confirms that visual features play a key role in achieving high accuracy in these situations.

Highly flexible recurrent state-space models can capture complex patterns in time series data, but typically assume a static and unchanging dynamic, a rare occurrence in real-world situations. To overcome this limitation, many systems exhibit patterns that are similar yet distinct, and can be described through a single underlying variable. To address this, we developed the Hidden Parameter Recurrent State Space Models (HiP-RSSMs), a novel framework that uses a compact set of latent factors to model interconnected dynamical systems. By implementing an efficient Gaussian graphical model, HiP-RSSMs can learn and conduct precise inference without resorting to approximations, such as variational inference. In our experiments, HiP-RSSMs consistently surpassed traditional state-space models and multi-task competitors on multiple demanding robotic tasks, in both real-world applications and simulations.

Independent unitarily invariant $N\times N$ random matrices exhibit expected asymptotic freeness to $O(N^{-2})$. Infinitesimal freeness in expectation is already known to result from this property. We've established an additional consequence: almost sure asymptotic freeness of type $B$ for unitarily invariant random matrices. This consequence leads to several secondary findings: the asymptotic cyclic monotonicity, and the derivation of the asymptotic free conditional distribution function from the unitarily invariant beta ensembles. Moreover, we prove the direct connection between the unitarily invariant beta ensembles and the Loewner differential equation.

We take a degree-2 cover of a genus-1 curve D over a non-hyperelliptic genus-3 curve C, in a field of characteristic not 2. We construct a genus-2 curve X, such that its Jacobian is connected to a product of the Jacobian of D and X's Jacobian, the Jacobian of C being an isogeny.

Determining the extent of polarization within social systems is vital to studying its effects on political structures. While numerous methods are employed to analyze polarization in social networks through structural evaluation, our analysis revealed that eight commonly used methods yield elevated polarization scores even in artificially constructed networks that closely mirror real-world networks in density and distribution. Furthermore, some of these methods proved sensitive to specific characteristics of polarized groups, such as degree distribution and size. We proposed introducing a standard normalization to mitigate these issues, alongside a comprehensive set of criteria for effective measurement of structural polarization. By normalizing the scores, the classification performance increased by up to 220%, and notably, the choice of measurement method became significantly less crucial, with most methods surpassing the previous best approach following normalization, thereby underscoring the paramount importance of standard normalization in the context of structural polarization measurement.

The analysis of multilayer networks has been utilized to model various dynamic systems, offering a more accurate representation than single-layer networks, albeit at the cost of increased analytical complexity. To overcome this challenge, we present a method for examining the dynamics of Kuramoto oscillators within multilayer networks by applying a joint matrix representation. This technique provides a compact representation of the multilayer system that maintains equivalent dynamics. As a result, we can determine solutions for the reduced system and then extend them to the multilayer network. Furthermore, we explore the impact of interlayer connections on the stability of these solutions. Our analysis reveals that certain multilayer configurations may exhibit greater stability than their corresponding single-layer counterparts.

Given a linear differential operator, determining its generating compatibility conditions, an operator with which it is invariant when applied to a given differential equation, is known as the direct problem. This process yields successive first-order operators for an n-dimensional manifold. The converse, an inverse problem, is to find the original differential operator when one of these compatibility operators is known. The compatibility operator can be parameterized by the original differential operator only if it defines a torsion-free differential module. The parametrization is minimal when this differential module has a vanishing differential rank. Notably, attempts to parameterize the Cauchy stress operator have been a subject of study for renowned scientists such as G.B. Airy, J.C. Maxwell, and A. Einstein. This work identifies a widespread misconception among them, mistakenly using the Einstein operator and confusing it with the Cauchy operator and the $div$ operator induced from the Bianchi operator. As an interesting aside, determining whether Einstein was aware of previous work is a historical puzzle.

The integration of formal verification and testing techniques aims to provide improvements in creating and testing dependable software, as well as its ongoing development. Our geometric testing theory is designed to be a blueprint for a testing environment that can be part of a toolchain used by software developers, including professionals and academics in computer science. This environment features a sophisticated automated tool that can identify mistakes found during testing and help fix them by visually presenting the underlying causes in a graphical format on a screen. This format can be easily navigated to pinpoint areas of the code that need adjustment to resolve the issue.

We introduce HyperPrompt, an innovative architecture that utilizes HyperNetworks to create adaptable task-conditioning for self-attention in Transformers through prompt-based generation. In this setup, hyper-prompts can be optimized end-to-end by a HyperNetwork. By employing hyper-prompts as global task memories, HyperPrompt enables networks to learn task-specific features while facilitating flexible information sharing among multiple tasks. Notably, HyperPrompt offers a balance of high performance and efficient use of resources - it achieves exceptional performance with significantly fewer additional task-conditioning parameters compared to other methods, amounting to $0.14\%$ of the parameters required, ultimately showcasing great computational efficiency.
