Assuming the observed data consist of independent realizations from $f(y|\theta_i)$ with weights $p_i$ representing the probabilities of observing $Y_i$, this paper establishes conditions and provides an estimator for consistent estimation of $\eta_G$. A novel method is introduced to estimate standard errors, with a proof of convergence in the asymptotic framework, demonstrated through simulation, and illustrated with sampling data.

Knowledge tracing has seen significant advancements through deep learning-based models, however the underlying factors behind their success remain poorly understood. A primary challenge lies in comparing these approaches, due to the lack of standardization in data preprocessing procedures and evaluation protocols. These inconsistencies hinder real-world applicability in educational settings. To address these limitations, we present PyKT, a comprehensive Python-based platform for validating deep learning knowledge tracing methods. This platform ensures a uniform data preprocessing procedure and protocol, thereby enabling more meaningful comparisons and facilitating the rapid development of novel deep learning knowledge tracing methods.

Given any manifold $M$, we demonstrate that a second-order elliptic differential operator $P$ possesses closed range in $C^\infty(M)$. Additionally, if the manifold $M$ does not consist of any compact components, it follows that $P$ is surjective within $C^\infty(M)$. This is accompanied by an exploration of its applications to Helmholtz decomposition.

Ten years ago, at the inaugural PxTP workshop, veriT's proof format debuted,  
which has undergone significant evolution ever since. veriT's proofs have found a  
wide range of applications and numerous solvers now generate proofs in this same  
format. As the next step in further improvement, we would like to hear feedback  
from the community to guide upcoming developments in this area. This feedback will  
be utilized in looking at the format's past progression, presenting the approach  
that guided its development, as well as the problems other solvers may experience  
in utilizing it.

As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce efficiency. The FedBuff algorithm mitigates this limitation by enabling asynchronous updates and securely aggregated data sharing, thus improving scalability while protecting user privacy. Building on the FedBuff framework for asynchronous learning, this study enhances existing research by relaxing the requirement that the gradient magnitude must remain within predefined bounds. Theoretical convergence rate analysis of the modified FedBuff algorithm considers factors like diverse data sets, varying batch sizes, and delay intervals.

Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition systems have achieved high accuracy, however, these systems demand considerable amounts of data and advanced computational power. Transfer learning has been proposed to overcome such challenges even across linguistic barriers, for example using a trained English model for German ASR. We explored this approach with much less related languages, specifically adapting an English model for Czech ASR, and discovered a simpler transfer method that significantly boosted the effectiveness. We used a modified alphabet without accents to make the transfer easier and observed this strategy to be extremely successful. Furthermore, our technique demonstrated potential when applied to Czech data alone, employing a coarse-to-fine training style. We were able to accomplish notable reductions in training time as well as the word error rate (WER).

Graph mining applications rely heavily on node embeddings that preserve structure and proximity. To test the validity of novel node embedding techniques, a limited range of benchmark datasets is typically used. In this study, a new diverse social network dataset, Twitch Gamers, has been created to provide a range of target attributes. The evaluation of the social network and the results of the node classification experiments confirm that Twitch Gamers can effectively assess the performance of novel node embedding algorithms.

Our study proposes that a previous observation made by Belle and BaBar of a complex spin state at around $1500$, which had been interpreted as a single entity or combination of multiple spin states, is now identified as the $\rho^0(1450)$ resonance seen in $\pi^+\pi^-$ channels with a confirmed mass of around $1447$ and width of approximately $257$.  Further analysis based on a detailed analysis of $B^0\to \gamma\gamma(\gamma*)^0$ decay modes by LHCb using a data set of $3.8\,{\rm fb}^{-1}$ leads to a exclusion of a mass range from $1380$ to $1550$ at the $90\%$ confidence level, thereby providing a precise constraint that supports only the $\rho^0(1450)$ interpretation for the structure at $1500$.  This conclusion is reached through analysis of $\bar{B}^0\to \bar{K}^0\Sigma(\Sigma^*)^0\to \bar{K}^+K^- \Sigma^{0*}\to K̄^+K^- K̄^-$ invariant mass distributions as well as through an analysis of $\bar{B}^0\to \bar{K}^0 \bar{K}^+K^-$ decays

Recent research suggests adding a new dimension to extra-dimensional gravity could lead to the existence of a dark dimension in the landscape. Combining this with the imposition of the Swampland program's constraints on scalar field charge, the intensity, and the entropy, the theory of string consistency suggests that the dark dimension should contain charged scalar fields and constitutes approximately 17% of dark matter in the form of primordial black holes. Research into the dynamics and observational evidence of these black holes suggests that they can explain the observed density of dark matter in the galactic centers and a phenomenon known as the core-cusp problem in galactic halos. The theoretical and empirical data support the hypothesis that these primordial black holes constitute a fraction of dark matter. The research also explores the impact of removing the extra dimension and how it affects the predicted fraction of primordial black holes, as well as the potential for detecting the evaporation of these black holes through their decay products and the characteristics of the waves produced by mergers, including the frequency at which this occurs. The research suggests that the presence of gas in the vicinity of dark matter halos containing these primordial black holes could allow for the detection of their evaporation, while the absence of this gas could hinder such observations. The research also predicts that primordial black holes with a mass ranging from 10^-9 to 10^2 times the mass of the Sun could comprise a fraction of dark matter, although the presence of the extra dimension may inflate this range. A novel algorithm for precise force control in series elastic actuators is introduced in this paper, centered on a cutting-edge force estimation technique called the transmission force observer. This approach was developed to enhance the inaccurate force readings caused by the nonlinear elastic transmission and sensor measurement errors of the actuators' deformation sensors. The study first critiques conventional SEA force sensing methods, examining their stochastic properties that ultimately enable accurate force control through the proposed transmission force observer. A critical parameter derived from system analysis is key in optimizing the performance of the force control system, guiding the selection of the optimal filter time constant for the low-pass filter used to smooth the force estimate. The proposed algorithm's effectiveness is validated via actual experiments conducted on an elastic actuator setup.

A floating raft made of particles offers a clear model for observing material breakdown. Due to the slow timescales, both how the particles move back to a more stable configuration and the formation of cracks within the raft can be measured precisely. When we extend a raft made of particles by expanding its surface of support, we see that its breaking pattern changes constantly based on the rate at which we are stretching it. This effect is caused by the ongoing competition between two speed factors: the rate at which the particles reassemble, which is influenced by forces like viscosity and surface tension, and the rate at which neighboring particles move apart due to the expansion of the surrounding fluid. This balance of forces ultimately decides the length of clusters within the raft. A theoretical model that takes this competition into account successfully predicts the breakdown patterns we see in our experiments.

We've analyzed a range of SU(Nc) gauge theories in 3D lattices that incorporate degenerate, multi-component complex scalar fields. These scalar fields are part of the fundamental representation of both the SU(Nc) gauge group and the global U(Nf) symmetry group. We've investigated their interactions within a general quartic potential that is compatible with the global and gauge symmetries. By analyzing minimum-energy configurations and performing Monte Carlo simulations, we've studied the phase diagrams, Higgs phases, and corresponding symmetry-breaking patterns. The influence of the quartic potential has also been assessed, while moving towards more favorable minimum-energy configurations of the scalar field occurs as a result of a transition from superconducting Higgs phases to non-superconducting ones, or even as a transition of the plasma as a result of screening by the plasma parameter.

Our novel TD learning approach overcomes several challenges robots encounter when navigating underwater.  By leveraging Gaussian Process regression, our model is particularly effective when data is limited and accesses prior knowledge to make informed predictions with few measurements.  To reduce the intricate nature of the value function, we have developed a sparse GP approximation within the TD learning framework.  The resulting algorithm is highly efficient in terms of computation and learning.  By incorporating a sparse GP into the policy, we have further simplified the learning process, making it more effective with fewer updates, while maintaining satisfactory performance.  Our results indicate these advancements are crucial for underwater navigation, enabling excellent outcomes even with significantly reduced training time.

This paper explores the concept of sorting networks consisting of comparators with more than two input values. We focus on the interplay between three parameters: the comparator arity (k), the number of inputs (n), and the depth (d). Our research highlights the previously studied relationships between these parameters, including a lower and upper bound for the required comparator arity (k) in relation to constant depth (d). Notably, we contribute upper bounds on k for specific constant depths (d=3 and d=4) as functions of n, demonstrating how sorting networks with 2-input comparators of depth 5 log_2(n) - 2 can be constructed, improving on the earlier bound of 5 log_2(n) - 3 log_2(log_2(n)) + O(1) established by Andriesse, Knauer, and Paulusson at CFG 2019. Furthermore, we show the connectivity of sorting networks with 3-input comparators of depth 4 log_3(n) + O(1) via a constant-depth comparator network.

We employ a 1+1+2 covariant semi-tetrad method to describe a static and spherically symmetric relativistic star comprising two fluids with anisotropic pressures, leading to the derivation of anisotropic Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations in covariant form. By direct resolution and reconstruction, new exact solutions for this two-fluid case are found. Additionally, three theorems applicable to the single-fluid scenario can be adapted to yield two-fluid solutions from their single-fluid counterparts.

Using recent observations, we create a set of models for a galaxy like the Milky Way. By combining collisionless and gaseous particle simulations, we observe that a bar forms in the center within one billion years, along with spiral arms composed of 2, 3, and 4-armed patterns. These features persist for at least 3 billion years in our simulations. However, we find that a bar won't develop if the galaxy's disk has a radial scale longer than 2.6 kiloparsecs. A compact bulge also prevents bar formation, as predicted. Our findings also indicate that a bar contributes to the maximum rotation curve in a galaxy's central regions due to its shape and orientation.

Galactic mergers significantly shape galaxy evolution, especially those involving massive galaxy combinations that significantly alter galaxy morphology. This study focuses on how magnetic fields affect major mergers involving abundant gas, using high-resolution simulations to examine the impact. Conducting this analysis within a realistic cosmic framework, this study employs advanced simulations to compare magnetic field effects on merging galaxies with and without magnetic field influence. Unlike previous non-realistic simulations, this study discovers that incorporating magnetic fields in simulations of massive galaxy mergers has a notable impact on how these galaxy combinations solidify. Although magnetic fields do not greatly alter general features, they have a notable effect on structural characteristics, forming extended discs and spiral patterns in simulations, whereas simulations without magnetic fields yield more compact, ring-like shapes. A separate investigation on resolution demonstrates that global features converge across various levels of resolution and physical modeling but reveals distinct differences in galaxy morphology at sufficient resolution, attributed to enhanced amplification of magnetic fields in high-resolution simulations, effectively impacting gas dynamics.

Our solution to the 2nd COVID-19 Severity Detection Competition has been successfully presented, where our goal was to classify chest CT images into Mild, Moderate, Severe, and Critical COVID-19 grades. To achieve this, we proposed a cutting-edge infection-aware 3D classification network called the Contrastive Mixup Classification network. This innovative approach involved initially training two segmentation networks to identify lung regions and inner lesions. These lesion masks were used in conjunction with the original CT scans to generate additional useful information. To rectify data imbalance, we incorporated weighted cross-entropy loss into our improved Contrastive Mixup Classification network. Consequently, our approach earned top honors with a Macro F1 Score of 51.76%, outperforming the baseline by a substantial 11.46%.

Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating more pseudo data to improve performance. In contrast, little work addresses the challenge of adapting GEC to new domains with limited resources. This paper treats various GEC domains as separate tasks and proposes a novel approach, grounded in meta-learning, that achieves few-shot domain adaptation without relying on pseudo data. Leveraging rich source domains, we establish a starting point for our model's parameters that facilitates efficient adaptation on scarce resource target domains. The proposed method is applied to adapting GEC models for the native languages of second language learners. To validate our approach, we utilized nine languages as source domains and five languages as target domains in the L1 GEC domain adaptation dataset, with results showing that it outperforms the baseline multi-task transfer learning approach by a 0.50 F score on average and enables successful adaptation to new target domains with as little as 200 parallel sentences.

Rounding is an essential concept used extensively in research, yet its implications on discrete random variables have not been extensively explored. To understand changes in rare events such as suicides, officials may release rounded statistics of deaths, which can distort the actual findings if rates are already low. In this research, we focus on estimating non-negative discrete variables using rounded averages, specifically when U equals the average of Y divided by n. Theoretical measures including the probability generating function, expected value, and variance are utilized to analyze how rounding impacts data and assess the impact on distribution parameter estimators. Our analysis reveals that in certain cases, rounding has a minimal effect but can severely distort results in other situations as demonstrated through practical applications. The simple techniques proposed are capable of mitigating the impact of rounding errors to some extent.

Researchers investigated the crystal and magnetic characteristics of the single-crystal, hexagonal GdInO3 through an integrated approach that combined experimental and theoretical analysis.  A centered honeycomb structure comprising triangular and honeycomb triangles within each layer defines this material, which displays significant interlayer coupling along the c-axis.  Using an effective spin-7/2 Hamiltonian, the researchers were able to explain the complex Gd3+ ground state via DFT and subsequent group theory analysis.  The resulting model accurately represented the primary features of the Gd3+ ground state, and the application of second-order perturbation theory yielded the primary exchange interactions.  A verifiable signature of the interlayer exchange interaction Jc was obtained by comparing the model to experimental data from inelastic neutron scattering, which demonstrated a characteristic energy that could not be accounted for with considering only the primary exchange interactions within the ab plane.  Furthermore, a local anisotropy parameter was derived from the analysis of inelastic neutron scattering data, and the results were compared to those from single-crystal anisotropy measurements.  This study contributes to the body of knowledge by being the first examination of the crystal and magnetic structure, as well as the interlayer exchange interaction Gd3+, in a centerd honeycomb antiferromagnet.

The task of allocating non-divisible goods to self-interested agents, where the valuation functions are additive, is examined in the context of the existence of Pure Nash Equilibria (PNE). Our analysis indicates that whether a PNE is attainable, it relies on whether the valuation functions satisfy a certain inequality relation. We establish that additive valuations meet this inequality, thereby guaranteeing the existence of PNE for such cases. Furthermore, we determine that whether a PNE is achievable for a specific set of valuations is an NP-complete problem when valuations have two outcomes, indicating limited fairness allocations are likely to result in PNE with such valuations. As a result, we propose randomized protocols to produce allocations that are both fair and possess a high probability of reaching PNE: we develop a deterministic, maximal-in-range proportional allocation method for two outcomes valuations that yields a PNE with a high probability; for envy-freeness, we provide two randomized protocols - one where we randomly select from maximal-in-range envy-free allocations, indicating an envy-free outcome exists in the case of VOS valuations, investigating the relationship between p-norm and Lp fairness notions; another based on the round-robin procedure for matroid-independent valuations, investigating the relationship between envy-free and p-norm fairness notions. We also prove limited fairness allocations are likely to possess p-norm fairness with expected guarantees of O(m^(p-1)) for all p > 1, impacting allocations made by

In our research, we diverge from the standard practice in unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) of employing a direct one-to-one correlation ('mapping') between source and target domains. Instead, we utilize stochastic translations to account for the inherent ambiguities in domain transformations. This strategy enables us to achieve better results by generating various outputs based on a single source image, thereby utilizing both accurate translations and data augmentation to handle visual variations, producing reliable target labels through the averaging of source predictions across multiple transformed versions of a single target image, and training and aggregating diverse target networks by regulating the degree of stochasticity in translations. Notably, our findings demonstrate notable improvements over strong recent baselines on two prominent UDA datasets for image classification, including up to a 3.7% increase in accuracy on the VisDA-2017 dataset.

UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in a substantial HII region located in the extreme outer rim of its disk. A comparative study with four similar spiral galaxies reveals that the unusual star-forming region in UGC 8839 is even more extraordinary. Contrary to typical hyper-stable disks where a substantial HII region should be insufficient to maintain the disk's stability, the disk of UGC 8839 exhibits exceptional stability. Dynamical analysis suggests that the disk of UGC 8839 closely resembles low-density, gas-rich disk scenarios, and likely retains potential for additional outer disk growth. Furthermore, it is deduced that the major attributes influencing star formation in the extreme outer disk of UGC 8839 are likely external, with the HII region probably being just one aspect of this environmental impact.

Researchers propose using paleo-detectors, an experimental technique, to detect dark matter. Unlike conventional detectors, which require massive and expensive set-ups, paleo-detectors utilize naturally occurring rocks with deep geological history that contain tiny damage tracks from dark matter interactions. Thanks to advancements in microscopy and the ability to study samples over billions of years, paleo-detectors can potentially offer more sensitive detection at significantly lower costs. This could significantly expand the range of validity for current detector technologies and even challenge the remaining dark matter parameter space. In this research, a thorough analysis of detection methods and achievable paleo-detector masses is performed and corresponding search regions in dark matter parameter space is calculated. Additionally, the possibility of collaborating with cosmochronology studies to find ideal detector samples and the potential of using multiple types of microscopy to minimize false positives from neutrino interactions is explored.

This paper introduces a novel form of leakage in modern encrypted databases, specifically 'update pattern leakage'. A formalized definition and security framework for DP-Sync are presented, leveraging differential privacy through 'DP update patterns'. A proposed framework, DP-Sync, builds upon existing database schemes by incorporating differential privacy-protected update patterns, ensuring the entire update history of outsourced data remains confidential.

The extensive use of Machine Learning (ML) in high-security sectors necessitates a transparent understanding of its methodology. Nonetheless, research into decoding ML models like Random Forest is in its nascent stages. To bridge this knowledge gap, we employ rigorous mathematical techniques and logical reasoning to create a pioneering method for explaining the predictions made by Random Forest. Our approach revolves around Minimal Unsatisfiable Cores and furnishes an exhaustive analysis for feature importance, encompassing both localized and broad aspects, along with adversarial sample examination. Empirical results across multiple datasets showcase the precision of our feature importance assessments. Furthermore, our method outperforms the current state-of-the-art adversarial analysis technique and offers the ability to generate user-centric reports that can inform recommendations in real-world scenarios.

Minimally invasive surgery has emerged as a highly effective treatment, allowing for non-invasive exploration of abdominal organs. Advances in medical technology, particularly high-definition cameras and sophisticated software, have enhanced its efficacy and paved the way for computer-assisted procedures. Although the process still faces technical challenges, we have investigated several popular deep learning approaches to improve automated detection and tracking of surgical instruments during laparoscopic surgery. The evaluation of our methods revealed that a novel deep learning network outperformed existing alternatives, yielding impressive accuracy and real-time processing capabilities. The exceptional performance of the model, characterized by high Dice coefficients and fast frame rates, signifies significant potential for its application in medical tool tracking.

Current public datasets for re-identifying individuals are limited due to the difficulties associated with labeling them. Despite the abundance of unlabeled surveillance footage that can be easily obtained, it's unclear how to effectively utilize this content to develop useful re-identification representations. Typically, existing methods focused on unsupervised and domain adaptation use publicly available datasets and then apply them to the target domain after removal of the labels, relying heavily on the relatively small size of the training data. This typically involves fine-tuning the method using the target domain's unlabeled data in order to achieve good results. By building upon recent advancements in self-supervised and contrastive learning that utilize large datasets without the need for labeling, our approach directly trains a re-identification system on the target domain using only the unlabeled surveillance footage. As a demonstration of potential, we also release the SSVE dataset for person re-identification, composed of unlabeled video content from 2888 camera views and containing 54394 video clips of 1687 unique individuals. By leveraging public annotation datasets, we also examine how contrastive learning ranks among other unsupervised methods such as cycle-consistent and auto-encoders, along with various techniques for combining them. By utilizing state-of-the-art pre-trained networks and advanced contrastive learning strategies on large datasets, our approach exhibits significant performance improvements of up to 200% when compared to baseline methods. This paper presents an original model that uses a unique threshold measurement formula in the Realized-GARCH model. The new framework utilizes a non-linear model that takes into account the 'leverage effect' and models the connection between realized volatility and hidden volatility. A specific estimation method was adopted, a simulation test was performed to evaluate its effectiveness. Furthermore, the paper conducts a practical study using real-world data, predicting Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall for various stock market indices with varying forecasting lengths. Results demonstrate the capability of the new framework to achieve competitive accuracy compared to established GARCH and Realized-GARCH type models.

Recent findings from global pulsar timing arrays suggest a nano-Hertz gravitational wave background signal remains elusive in current data. Nevertheless, enhanced datasets are expected to yield statistically significant evidence in the future. This study endeavors to eliminate sampling bias in data analysis. By examining various configurations of nested samplers and traditional Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods, we aim to identify the time efficiency and consistency of these sampling techniques on pulsar timing array data. Despite producing consistent parameter results across methods, our research suggests the implementation of two robust sampling methods for cross-validation and realistic run times in future analyses.

Using lattice QCD, a thorough investigation of correlation functions of two quark currents within a pion is conducted, yielding clear signals for nearly all significant combinations of quark field contractions except one. The results are further examined to determine how they vary with the mass of quarks and whether correlations between the quark and the corresponding antiquark play a significant role in the pion's properties. Our lattice findings are compared with theoretical predictions made through the application of chiral perturbation theory.

Evaluating protoplanetary disk evolution is closely tied to understanding how
mass accretion rates are influenced by a star and its disk properties.
However, accurately using observed relations in this context is hampered by
not properly accounting for variations in mass accretion rates, a problem
especially prevalent in earlier stages of star formation. Conversely, we found
large-scale fluctuations in mass accretion rates of one specific object, XX
Cha, and how this could affect our current understanding of T Tauri star
systems. Comparing this finding to earlier research, we concluded that not
factoring in mass accretion variability could lead to overestimating the
range of mass accretion rates by up to an order of magnitude. Additionally,
not considering this variability might cause a shift of up to 0.5 dex in the
established relationship between log$\dot{M}$ and the color index ($c$), a
parameter derived from spectral energy distributions.

This study explores how uncertainty about chance influencing job success and earnings impacts redistribution policies in a diverse group of people. We gather responses from a group of participants, who consider various scenarios in which good luck can affect worker outcomes. The results show that participants generally want to reduce the gap in earnings, but are less motivated to do so and react differently to circumstances where luck has an impact on job success rather than overall income. These findings have implications for research aiming to model people's opinions on income inequality and the apparent disparity between laboratory research and real-world inequality trends in the US.

Removing a subspace from a partial flag results in another partial flag consisting of fewer components. This action induces a mapping $\pi : X \to X'$ between corresponding flag varieties, which essentially discards information to yield a coarser partial flag structure in $X'$. In a context of stable maps, for sufficiently large degrees, a key geometric object - associated with maps that target Schubert varieties $X_i$ - exhibits the structure of a rational connection over its parameter space in $X'$, which now displays multiple distinct components. By applying the block group action to this object at each point, we obtain canonical measurements that satisfy fundamental consistency conditions seeles when maps of lower degrees are obtained through composition with these maps of higher degrees, thereby establishing our framework for defining quantum $K$-theory for certain types of flag varieties and proving the associated fundamental consistency principles quantum $K$-theoretic атрола.

The development of modern machine learning applications is centered on data and is complicated by a critical issue: understanding the influence of data quality on training. The problem of pinpointing which training examples are responsible for a trained model's inaccuracies or biases has gained significant attention over the past decade. The computation of the Shapley value for training examples with respect to validation accuracy and model fairness has become a popular framework for tackling this issue. Although recent studies have made progress in computing the Shapley value for a single machine learning model in isolation, they fail to account for a end-to-end machine learning pipeline, consisting of multiple interdependent components such as feature selection, preprocessing, and model selection. This paper extends the computation of the Shapley value to a single machine learning pipeline and introduces an efficient method for computing the Shapley value for training examples with respect to model performance. The results from our experiments, which include analyses of dataset size, feature selection, and preprocessing, demonstrate that our efficient computation outperforms previous methods. The debugging of machine learning models, which involve identifying training examples that contribute to model inaccuracies or biases, can be accomplished by ranking training examples based on their Shapley values, as shown in our empirical evaluations of real-world datasets.

We explored possible connections between the number of radio sources observed within 22 galaxy clusters from the MAVERIC survey and factors like collision rates among stars within those clusters, the presence of binary systems, and mass segregation. Our analysis revealed a correlation between radio source counts and collision rates that exceeded significance at 2.6 sigma in data blinding tests, yet this correlation decreased to one significant sigma when considering binary systems and binary mergers of more massive objects. Given that binary binaries are more prevalent in the core regions of these clusters, our findings imply that star collisions, specifically those involving more massive stars and their subsequent impact on surrounding matter, may be responsible for the majority of radio source activity within a significant margin of error, comprising about 70 percent of the core activity. Moreover, we discovered that radio source density correlates with density squared in the core regions, but only shows a linear relationship with mass segregation when adjusted for the movement of stars to higher density areas, suggesting that star movements alone cannot account for radio source activity, particularly in the core regions.

We investigate a widespread challenge in analyzing complex graph systems: their representation often hides crucial interdependencies among entities, resulting in an ambiguous and incomplete understanding. Scholars have proposed hypergraphs to address this limitation, yet they suffer from an excessive number of redundant connections. To develop a clearer, more comprehensive hypergraph representation, we devise a supervised learning approach to reconstruct them. Our method leverages available two-node relationships and historical data to predict the more significant three-node connections. To this end, we develop a sophisticated hypergraph convolutional network that fuses the proposed relationships. Experimental results reveal that our model achieves superior performance compared to classical graph learning techniques and random hypergraph sampling, showcasing the significance of selective, meaningful hypergraph connections. Furthermore, applications to real-world scenarios, such as identifying spam emails and fake news articles, demonstrate the efficacy of our method.

We propose an advanced concept for measuring directional emission in microcavity lasers. Initially, entropy in the polar far-field profile effectively gauges the degree of unidirectional light release, outperforming previous methods which struggle with variation. Secondly, we introduce a phenomenological angle for measuring emission directionality, but its practical application is limited to straightforward cases due to the inability to handle complex structures. Conversely, entropy based on semi-marginal probability in the Cartesian coordinate achieves comparable results and is also adaptable to emissions with complex structures.

The scattering of coherent light from heated alkali metals in a range of 350-450 Kelvin is examined in detail, and atomic spacings are measured in terms of wavelength from approximately 0.7 lambda to 0.1 lambda. A comprehensive theoretical framework models thermal alkali metals as groups of interacting radiating dipoles, and demonstrates that photon correlation data can be accurately predicted through random atomic pair positioning. Experiments confirm our findings with positive outcomes. Adjusting key variables within these experiments offers opportunities to investigate distinct regimes of photon behavior.

Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among the agents' learned behavior. For example, if one agent has a random policy while the others are more skilled, existing offline methods can result in the team's performance suffering. To tackle this problem, we present a novel offline learning framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) that explicitly considers the diversity of individual trajectories. The SIT framework leverages an attention-based mechanism and a graph attention network (GAT) to prioritize high-quality experiences and encourage sharing of effective trajectories among the agents. Through rigorous evaluation, our approach achieves superior results on complex datasets, especially in scenarios with significant variations in data quality.

We developed a novel approach for registering MV images, utilizing a Convolutional Neural Network, in both 2D and 3D. Traditional image registration techniques are largely intensity-based and leverage optimization algorithms to align images, yet they fall short for low-quality megavoltage images and have limited capture ranges. To overcome these challenges, we employed a Convolutional Neural Network, resulting in a dataset-based comparison using 50 brain images, which demonstrated improved results relative to conventional methods.

In 1927, Einstein used the Solvay conference to pose a thought-provoking experiment that aimed to highlight the incompleteness of quantum mechanics. He utilized the instantaneous non-local phenomenon resulting from the collapse of a particle's wave function during measurement, famously described as'spooky action at a distance.' Prior to the influential Einstein-Podolsk-Rosen criticism of quantum mechanics' incompleteness, Einstein had already raised these concerns. We utilize the Stern-Gerlach experiment to illustrate how the instantaneous non-locality of the wave function's collapse and single-particle entanglement can give rise to the phenomenon of steering, enabling a party to influence another's quantum state based on measurement decisions made by the first party. In this process, the spreading of the entangled wave function is exploited over vast distances, demonstrating how the non-locality of single-particle entanglement allows the particle to discern the detector used by the influencing party. Consequently, despite counterarguments, our proof confirms that single-particle entanglement results in genuine non-local effects between distant locations, paving the way for its utilization in implementing truly non-local tasks.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques and improved information systems within Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) has yielded substantial benefits, albeit with heightened risks of security breaches and compromised privacy. As IoVs technology continues to evolve, there's growing interest in privacy preservation methodologies that adapt to these changes. Federated Learning has shown promise in safeguarding IoVs data and addressing concerns about security and privacy, whereas Blockchain technology presents possibilities for secure and verifiable data management. This paper conducts an in-depth review of Blockchain-Enabled Federated Learning frameworks for IoVs, exploring potential problems, viable solutions, and future directions. This comprehensive survey can serve as a foundation for developing novel BC-Enabled FL solutions to address various IoVs data privacy challenges and scenarios.

V392 Persei, classified as a dwarf nova that underwent a classic nova explosion in 2018, is an extraordinary object whose extreme evolution over nearly three years has been closely observed.  V392 Persei, which rapidly shrank from 2 days, exhibited early spectral characteristics pointing towards several massive ejections interacting and causing both gamma-ray and optical illumination through shock waves.  V392 Persei entered its Sun-constrained phase soon after its eruption but upon exiting it entered its nebular stage with evidence of the super-soft X-ray stage's lingering effects.  Post-nova observations of the optical spectrum showed the gradual decline of the orbital velocity, ushering in an extended intermediate phase whose duration will be determined by future spectral observations.  Furthermore, the system's rapid evolution caused V392 Persei to exhibit notable shifts in its classification, evolving from a dwarf nova to an intermediate nova and eventually an optical transient with gamma-ray emissions before and during its nova phase.  This study aims to provide an extensive overview of V392 Persei's diverse spectral characteristics using optical, X-ray, and gamma-ray observations, which will help inform future theoretical models.

In quantum computing, generating the entanglement of any number of qubits in a single operation has significant implications for error correction, particularly when combined with stabilizer measurements. Utilizing a single multi-qubit gate instead of several two-qubit gates in parity-check circuits is demonstrated using the toric code, resulting in improved fault tolerance when applying a five-qubit gate over individual two-qubit gates in the context of quantum error correction, particularly when applied to ion qubits susceptible to spontaneous photon scattering, leading to lower logical error rates in the presence of bit-flip and decoherence noise.

A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to construct codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Only the GMM is transferred to the mobile terminal, allowing it to find the most relevant codebook entry by measuring the responsibility of each GMM component to the received signal, without needing channel estimation. Feedback is transmitted as the index of the most responsible component and corresponding codebook entry, leading to enhanced performance over traditional approaches, notably in scenarios with limited pilot data transmission.

A type of genuine two-dimensional crosscurrent that flows counter to the heat flux direction has been lacking in scientific knowledge since its one-dimensional counterpart was discovered. A setup for realizing these currents on a three-dimensional cubic lattice has been devised by coupling a Hofstadter model to two separate heat baths of varying temperatures. Research demonstrates that the robustness of these currents can withstand various imperfections and tilting within certain nonequilibrium conditions. Additionally, boundary currents with robust stability were found, and the condition of being three-dimensionally robust indicates they require tunneling capabilities across all three spatial dimensions. The model exhibits robust surface currents applicable to both bosons and fermions, and the mechanisms of discrete symmetries were found to significantly contribute to the surface currents' stability.

For asymptotically flat spacetimes, where light is emitted at a distance from the gravitational source, research indicates that the Bondi mass aspect must satisfy specific requirements to reach the point of infinity without obstruction. In general relativity, such constraints result in an upper limit on the mass change rate in relation to the speed of light and gravitational constant, leading to an interesting insight into Dyson's maximum luminosity theorem. In contrast, the conditions under which scalar gravitational waves in Brans-Dicke theory allow light to escape infinity without being overpowered by rapid mass loss.

We examine the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytical model for the early universe. Our framework accounts for the movement of Population III binary remnants during the formation of the universe's structure and identifies which of these remnants fall into nuclear star clusters through gravitational interaction with field stars. Following their formation, we employ a modified version of the SHARC code to investigate how these remnants concentrate in the center of the universe and make gravitational waves. Our study reveals that 0.1 percent of Population III binary remnants form the first nuclear star clusters within the universe and many of these will produce observable signals with third-generation gravitational wave detectors. However, the detection of these remnants will depend heavily on their formation rate, with a range of outcomes possible from silent universes to abundant gravitational waves detectable by detectors such as Cosmic Explorer.

The primary objective of the Gravitational wave high-energy Electromagnetic Counterpart All-sky Monitor (GECAM) is to observe various Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRB) that arise from the merger of compact binary stars or the collapse of massive stars, which can also generate gravitational waves. To test and calibrate the performance of GECAM's organic scintillator detectors, a portable GRB simulator has been developed using high-luminosity LED light sources. This device can replicate the intensity and duration variations seen in real GRB observations. With a total throughput of 105 photons per second equivalent to a 1 m² area, the simulator is capable of emulating faint GRB events and can be easily operated with control software on a laptop computer. The simulator was used to test GECAM over two nights and its intensity measurements were compared with virtual GRB observations made by the Cherenkov Burst Telescope (CBTE), a virtual instrument of the Cherenkov Telescope Array (CTA). While some large discrepancies were noticed in certain tests, the simulator successfully demonstrated that GRB-like observations could be emulated for both GECAM and CBTE.

This article investigates the semigroups of composition operators on BMOA-type spaces, specifically on BMOA_p and its analogue VMOA_p. BMOA_p is a part of the family of F(p,q,s) spaces introduced by R. Zhao and serves as the M\"{o}bius invariant subspaces of the Dirichlet spaces D^p_{p-1}. Our focus lies in analyzing the maximal subspace of strong continuity for semigroups of operators, exploring sufficient and necessary conditions on the infinitesimal generator of phi for the semigroup [phi_t, BMOA_p] to equal VMOA_p. We also establish the connection between the maximal subspace of strong continuity and the Volterra-type operators T_g, specifically examining which symbols g make T_g bounded or compact from BMOA to BMOA_1, while also investigating the relationship between compactness and weak compactness of T_g on BMOA_p when 1 < p < 2.

Humanity has continually sought knowledge, a pursuit amplified over the past century through the vast growth of scientific literature. However, despite employing metrics such as citation counts and impact factors, it remains unclear how a discipline's knowledge amount correlates with productivity, specifically how the value of new knowledge varies with new contributions. To address this question, researchers analyzed more than 13 million articles spanning 35 disciplines from the years 1960 to 2009, discovering a consistent disproportion between scientific productivity and knowledge amount, typically observed as an inverse relationship, often depicted as a "productivity pyramid." This phenomenon suggests that random chance plays a significant role in determining the value of a scientific contribution, suggesting that competition in scientific endeavors is more about luck than capability, and that expanding the pool of qualified contenders is more beneficial than attempting to increase the success rate of existing ones.

In this study, we examine the security risks associated with wireless communication systems that use dual hop OFDM technology. To mitigate this issue, we analyze two main cases: one involving a single user with a single relay, and another with multiple users and relays. The primary goal of this investigation is to determine optimal power allocation methods across various frequencies in order to enhance end-to-end data transmission security while adhering to power consumption constraints at both the sender and relay nodes. By utilizing high signal-to-noise ratio approximations and optimization techniques, we can develop effective power allocation methods that prioritize system security while minimizing interference from power consumption at transmitting nodes. Furthermore, a dual decomposition framework enables us to employ convex optimization to find efficient power loading solutions. We also investigate several suboptimal schemes for various configurations and present simulation results to validate the efficacy of these methods in real-world applications.

Two-dimensional systems with robust edge currents due to large Chern numbers offer a wealth of chiral modes related to their topological invariants. In photonic configurations, these edge currents translate to stable multi-mode waveguides that naturally protect the topological properties of the system. In our research, we combine these photonic setups with quantum sources, using a Harper-Hofstadter model to illustrate scenarios where quantum emitters display nearly quantized emission rates. These increased emission rates can be harnessed for faster communication between the emitters via exchange interactions, resulting in nearly qubit-independent entanglement generation. Notably, our findings show nearly protection of this entanglement from errors in the waveguide. Furthermore, we find that topological protection facilitates reliable quantum data bus functionality.

In the complex context of an urban intersection with automated and human-driven vehicles, we explore an essential challenge: generating safe pathways for automated vehicles. Our research focuses on preventing rear-end collisions when a connected vehicle's human-driven leader approaches the yellow and red phases of the traffic light. We've developed a predictive control system that can instantly forecast how the preceding human driver operates and utilize this prediction to create a safety-oriented pathway in a limited timeframe. The performance of this framework has been tested using a simulation and we assess its reliability.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months.

Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been highly effective in various sequence analysis tasks but suffer from limitations in their practical application due to their size. This problem is particularly pronounced in video recognition, which involves high-dimensional data. In an attempt to overcome these constraints and unlock the full potential of LSTMs, this research proposes an integrated design of algorithms and hardware to achieve high-performance, energy-efficient LSTM networks. At the algorithmic level, a new LSTM structure called FDHT-LSTM is developed, which significantly reduces model complexity without sacrificing accuracy. In addition to this optimized algorithm, a customized hardware platform is also designed to efficiently execute the FDHT-LSTM model by reducing memory access operations and enabling parallel matrix calculations. Experimental results indicate that the proposed framework outperforms existing methods in video recognition, exhibiting superior performance in terms of model size and computational efficiency. Furthermore, the energy efficiency benefits of this integrated design are highlighted through extensive evaluations on multiple datasets, demonstrating significant improvements in energy performance when compared to both traditional and state-of-the-art LSTM models.

Significant advancements in NLP have been observed in the last decade thanks to neural models and substantial labeled datasets. However, NLP models are often hindered by a reliance on extensive data availability, hindering their application to resource-constrained settings and unique tasks necessitating large-scale labeling. As a means of enhancing NLP data efficiency, data augmentation techniques have been investigated in recent years. A systematic examination of data augmentation in NLP under low-labeled data settings has been lacking until now, resulting in difficulty in comprehending the efficacy of diverse methods in various contexts. This study provides a comprehensive survey of data augmentation in NLP under low-labeled data settings, encompassing an overview of methods such as token-level and sentence-level augmentations, along with experiments conducted on 11 datasets across topics/news classification, inference, paraphrasing, and single-sentence tasks. Our research enables the formulation of recommendations to guide practitioners in selecting suitable augmentations tailored to different settings and highlights the current limitations and potential future pathways in this research area.

The concept of the Weak Gravity Conjecture is often expressed through its effect on the mass-to-charge ratio of a particle. An alternative formulation, the convexity weak gravity conjecture, examines how the charge of a particle changes in relation to its mass. Our research demonstrates that scalar and spinor particles with masses, charges, and form factors that maintain a convex relationship between mass and the square of the charge, can be consistently extended to a broader range of values, due to a fundamental property of effective field theories. This consistent behavior is characteristic of many scenarios proposed for the breakdown of an EFT and suggests that the convexity of the mass-to-charge ratio is a essential criterion that needs to be met in order to distinguish a phenomenon described by the Weak Gravity Conjecture from another possible explanation, such as the formation of a bound state or the emergence of an infrared effect. The formation of a bound state triggered by increasing the charge of a particle imposes the constraint that both the charge and the mass of a particle must be an equal value. The application of this criterion to the study of the spectrum of higher-dimensional black holes and the formulation of the convexity of the charge form factor leads to a potential expression of this criterion within the framework of four-dimensional scattering amplitudes.

To stabilize the estimation of ground and excited states on a quantum computer, we modify the quantum imaginary time evolution (QITE) to utilize the model space. This model-space QITE method iteratively expands the model space while maintaining its orthogonality, enabling simultaneous description of multiple states. We enhance model-space QITE by integrating the quantum Lanczos algorithm, which boosts its convergence rate. In simulations, our approach outperforms both standard quantum Lanczos and the folded-spectrum QITE in calculating excited states. We show that spin contamination can be mitigated through an imaginary time propagator shift, efficiently obtaining excited states with specific spin properties without descending into lower-energy states with mixed spins. Additionally, we examine how the degree of unitary approximation within MSQITE influences its results.

Given a Noetherian local ring with a specific prime characteristic and its primary ideal in terms of an $\mathfrak{m}$-primary parameter, we establish criteria for $F$-rationality based on the tight Hilbert function of that ideal. These criteria make use of a specific polynomial and its coefficient. Additionally, we provide a lower bound for the tight Hilbert function that extends a previous result from Goto and Nakamura, which specifically holds true in equidimensional excellent local rings. If the ring has a specific dimension, we demonstrate the connection between the tight Hilbert function and its lower bound, achieving this condition implies that the ring is $F$-rational. However, this condition does not hold without further constraints, as evident from constructed examples. Based on the ring's properties and test elements, we find formulas to compute those elements' valuations, which have implications for detecting $F$-rationality in certain semilocal rings.

The rapid transformation of the electricity sector necessitates innovative ancillary services that guarantee the stability and dependability of the electricity network. Unfortunately, evaluations of ancillary services often fail to account for the intricate interplay in the market. Our proposed framework assesses an expansion in ancillary services adoption through a robust general equilibrium model of market interactions. It highlights and visualizes key effects of this change, including supply and demand for goods, ancillary services provision, and feedback loops. Using a practical example, we show how an increase in tax revenue from ancillary services can influence these interconnections. The model can also aid in policy design by providing insights into ancillary services and interplay interplays. Specifically, it reveals that ancillary services provision may decrease due to higher tax rates, which can in turn lead to reduced consumption and lower tax revenue.

R. K. Singh and the author previously introduced the concepts of upper and lower prime valuation for a polynomial $f\in K[x]$, denoted as $
u^{upper}(f)$ and $
u^{lower}(f)$, based on the field $K$ and variable $x$. A composition of polynomials $f_1,\dots, f_r\in K[x]$ was then shown to satisfy the inequality $
u^{lower}(f_1\circ \dots \circ f_r)(x) \ge \sum_{i=1}^r 
u^{lower}(f_i)(x)$, confirming a conjecture made by M. Giuli and G. Zappa. This work also establishes the formula $\sum_{i=1}^r 
u^{lower}(f_i)(x) = \sum_{i=1}^r 
u^{lower}(f_i)(f_1\circ \dots \circ f_{i-1})(x)$ for compositions, with conditions of equality explored. Similarly, the equality $
u^{upper}(f_1\circ \dots \circ f_r)(x) = \sum_{i=1}^r 
u^{upper}(f_i)(x)$ holds under specific criteria, with broader implications.

To study non-resonant Higgs boson pair production in the $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ channel at the LHC using the matrix element method, we examine how to differentiate the Higgs boson pair signal from the dominant irreducible top quark pair background. Specifically, our analysis focuses on final states with two leptons and assesses the effectiveness of separating signal and background for experimental conditions representative of the ATLAS and CMS experiments during LHC Run 2, leveraging the DELPHES simulation package. As a result, we were able to achieve a $0.26\%$ top quark pair background suppression, corresponding to a $34\%$ Higgs boson pair signal efficiency.

We calculate one-loop corrections to the Standard Model process of a Z boson emitting a Higgs boson, considering extended scalar sector scenarios for the Standard Model, including inert doublets and various triplets, quintuplets, and septuplets with different new scalar SU(2)L representations. These new scenarios are expected to be probed at a precision of a part in 10^4 by future e+e- colliders due to precise measurements of σ(e+e- → Zh) that complement searches for the Standard Model scalar triplet. Additionally, we consider radiative corrections to the photon decay of the Higgs boson, correcting a recent result for the SM and exploring how the new scalar sectors affect the h → γγ decay. These precise studies of σ(e+e- → Zh) and the h → γγ decay complement each other and our findings are relevant for future research at the Large Hadron Collider, the Compact Muon Solenoid, the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider, and potential future muon colliders.

Saturn's polar atmosphere is characterized by seasonal variations of large warm whirlpools north of 75 degrees latitude. The strongest of these appear during Saturn's summer and disappear in the winter. The extensive exploration of the Saturn system enabled by the Cassini spacecraft has facilitated a comprehensive study of the formation of the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex through the application of infrared spectroscopy. By analyzing this phenomenon, researchers were able to identify the vortex's peak strength in April 2014, which lasted until July of the same year. During this period, the absence of molecular hydrogen escaping from the atmosphere's edge maintained the vortex's integrity, despite the loss of solar energy in 2014. As a result, observations revealed the formation of a polar stratospheric "hexagon" during the peak of the vortex's strength. Additionally, models have predicted the existence of a vortex "shield" lasting into the following spring. Now, with evidence supporting both predictions, they are regarded as reality. Furthermore, the complexity of six-fold symmetry in the hexagon seems to be reinforced by the presence of a similar stratospheric feature.

This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under the influence of a focusing nonlinearity with mass-supercritical properties, in a domain exterior to a compact convex obstacle in a higher-dimensional space. We demonstrate that solutions with negative energy will inevitably collapse within a finite time period. Additionally, under the assumption that the nonlinearity is not too strongly energy-dependent and given specific symmetry conditions, we establish the same optimal blow-up criterion found by Holmer and Roudenko for solutions in an infinite domain. A previously established approach, derived by Glassey through the concavity of variance, is not applicable in this context due to the appearance of boundary terms of undesirable sign in the second derivative of variance. Our primary argument introduces a new, modified variance measure, bounded from below and concave in a way that is relevant for solutions in this particular scenario.

We provide a novel proof that local characteristic-zero, semi-parametric embeddings for a polynomial variety defined over the integers have an equivalent form to local positive-characteristic reductions of the variety for nearly all prime numbers.

The manner in which the surface of materials is terminated has significant implications for their physical characteristics. Investigating the metal-insulator transition in V$_2$O$_3$ films necessitates a deep comprehension of the effect of surface termination.  Our studies achieved varying surface terminations in V$_2$O$_3$ films using low energy electron diffraction and photoemission spectroscopy, which led us to a key finding - depending on the surface termination, the metal-insulator transition may be suppressed, hindered, or fully preserved.  Our results are consistent withIndentation of the underlying structure induced by surface layers as the primary factor behind this phenomenon.  As a consequence, our study highlights the critical role of surface geometry in controlling the metal-insulator transition in magnetic oxides, which may have implications for the metal-insulator transition in other similar materials.

Our study uncovers new features of non-equilibrium behavior in quantum double dark-soliton states for one-dimensional repulsive boson gases. We find a specific scaling of Bose-Einstein condensation fractions in ground states that can be used to analyze quasi-condensation in weakly coupled quantum double dark-soliton states. We first demonstrate the precise time-dependent density profile of a quantum double dark-soliton state via the Bethe ansatz method. Next, we derive an effective macroscopic wave function for these states by calculating the amplitude and phase of the field operator's correlation, showing that quasi-condensation arises from fluctuations around dark solitons. For weak interactions, this quasi-condensation behavior aligns with thermal gas condensation. Finally, we numerically simulate the time evolution of quantum double dark-soliton states and our proposed quasi-condensation formula, finding excellent agreement with these results.

We create a linearisation functor for supermanifolds using extended differential calculus, which preserves the structure of split structures. This innovation allows us to introduce the concept of polarisation for fiberwise-linear superbundles and demonstrate that polarised superbundles can be regarded as extensions of complex bundles within a specific category. A key feature of this new approach within extended differential geometry is its reliance on linear algebra rather than super algebra. Additionally, we provide an alternative, more elementary description of supermanifolds that mirrors the extended differential calculus framework.

This informal note begins by illustrating some technical concepts, including the re-normalization of measures on orbital integrals from the works of Langlands, Frenkel-Langlands-Ng\^o, and Altug's research on Beyond Endoscopy. We discuss specific measures related to algebraic tori and explain how they relate to Tamagawa numbers. We then examine the GL2 case in depth. Additionally, the appendix by Matthew Koster clarifies the connection between the geometric measure of orbits and Kirillov's measure of co-adjoint orbits within the dual space of certain Lie algebras, including sl2 and so3.

The interaction between light and matter is used in various spectroscopic techniques to extract details about a sample's molecular, atomic, or nuclear components. Although scattered light conveys both amplitude and phase information, this phase information is frequently lost during standard intensity measurements, yet it is crucial for reconstructing essential details of a target, as evident from applications like coherent x-ray imaging. A novel algorithm is introduced that allows for retrieving phase information from two-dimensional time- and energy-resolved spectra, a feature we demonstrate with x-ray scattering off M\"ossbauer nuclei using a synchrotron radiation source. The knowledge gained through phase information also leads to accurate reconstruction of energy spectra from experimental data, a level of precision that cannot be achieved with other methods. Our approach provides a useful data analysis tool, offering a beneficial impact on x-ray quantum optics and M\"ossbauer spectroscopy that employs synchrotron radiation.

By linking quantum error correcting codes to models of disordered classical statistical mechanics and examining the phase diagram of these models, researchers have found a valuable tool for studying how these codes resist errors under various noise conditions. This study expands this mapping to account for realistic faulty quantum circuits when describing quantum error correcting codes. First, based on a detailed circuit noise model, we develop a strongly correlated classical spin model corresponding to each circuit noise scenario. This approach is illustrated using the quantum repetition code, where we simulate the impact of periodically malfunctioning stabilizer readout circuits. We utilize Monte Carlo simulations to investigate the phase diagram resulting from these interactions, and our findings are compared with the performance of a minimum-weight perfect matching decoder. This research provides a method for assessing the fundamental error thresholds of quantum error correcting codes, independently of any specific decoding strategies, and could help inform the design of near-term quantum computing hardware.

Recent theoretical predictions stating that group VI elemental monolayers can't be in the form of a honeycomb lattice structure have been disputed by new experimental findings. In this study, it's been found that incorporating oxygen into these monolayers, specifically tellurene, makes them dynamically stable and topologically non-trivial in the form of a honeycomb lattice. Oxygen functionalization brings about unique filtering effects on the orbits, breaks spatial symmetry, and produces the desired exotic quantum properties. A key characteristic of this system is its large-gap of around 0.36 eV, alongside isolated Dirac cones on the edges which indicate potential applications for room temperature spin-transport. Investigations of the spin Hall conductivity and berry curvatures show high conductivity when compared to other Xene materials. These properties can be quantified with the Z2 invariant and Chern number both being 1. A practical implementation of this is demonstrated in strain engineered hBN/TeO/hBN quantum wells that exhibit a significant non-trivial gap of 0.11 eV. Oxygen functionalization brings robust and stable electronic properties that could facilitate viable spintronic applications despite potential surface oxidation.

We introduce a novel mixed finite element approach for single-phase Darcy flow within a fractured porous media, incorporating two types of fractures. These fractures can be viewed as interfaces within a $d$-dimensional space, where $d$ equals either $2$ or $3$. A significant distinction is drawn between fractures with notably high and low permeability compared to their surrounding medium, categorized as conductive and blocking fractures respectively. Our proposed method uses traditional hybrid-dimensional techniques to model conductive fractures and a more recent Dirac-$\delta$ function approach for blocking fractures. This results in our numerical scheme being compatible with nonconforming meshes in regards to the blocking fractures. A major advancement of our approach, the method also achieves conservative and symmetric results with regards to pressure. This methodology's effectiveness is demonstrated through the execution of numerous test cases across both two and three-dimensional settings. Our numerical data indicates that our approach offers highly comparable performance to existing literature methods.

A comprehensive examination of a spin-triplet superconducting device, which involves a spiral magnetic arrangement, is conducted. The underlying metal exhibits unique magnetic characteristics that may arise due to competing isotropic exchanges or an asymmetrical magnetic arrangement. Depending on its anisotropy, the metal can transition between spiral and uniform magnetization orders. A specific type of magnetic arrangement known as the B20 structure further contributes to the device's operation, influencing the long-range pairing of superconducting electrons under intense exchange fields. However, numerical simulations demonstrate that an unusual orientation-dependent effect can be utilized to control the device's behavior at moderately low exchange fields. Consequently, a significant amplification of the device's effect is achieved when specific parameters such as exchange splitting and spiral period are comparable to the superconducting coherence length.

Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in cognitive science and the social and physical sciences. However, comparing model evidence between complex models remains a challenge due to issues like model saturation and the computational intensity required for hypothesis comparison. In this paper, we explore the use of Bayes factors for comparing models of human decision making and address several critical aspects of their application. Specifically, the robustness of Bayes factors to variations in experimental conditions, the utility of Savage-Dickey Bayes factors in conjunction with empirical Bayes model comparisons, and the feasibility of using Markov chain Monte Carlo methods for hypothesis comparison. As part of our analysis, a Python library called bay workflow is introduced to facilitate the implementation of these strategies. We provide an illustrative example of Bayesian hypothesis comparison for perceptual sensitivity using Bay workflow and demonstrate the potential for these techniques to be applied to a wide range of research areas.

Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on existing datasets used for classification tasks. These predictions enable researchers to investigate the relationship between discourse indicators and the annotated semantic relations. Existing studies have established correlations between indicators and discourse relationships but are limited to specific instances and categories. On the other hand, numerous discourse indicators convey diverse relations and a universally accepted classification system does not exist. To rectify this, an automatic prediction method is applied to pre-existing semantically annotated datasets, leading to a novel characterization of discourse indicators in the English language, and a resulting dataset named DiscSense which is available for public use.

We investigate the properties of a negatively charged nitrogen-vacancy center in diamond under high-temperature and vacuum conditions.  By combining optical detection of magnetic resonance (ODMR) and optical spectroscopy, we measure the 1s and 2s excited states of the nitrogen atom, as well as the nitrogen ground state, across a high temperature range (300K to 450K).  Our experiments indicate that the electronic transitions are relatively stable over this temperature range, with shift rates below 10^-4 eV/K, in contrast to other qubits based on superconducting circuits or atomic ensembles that are more susceptible to thermal fluctuations.  However, as temperatures rise beyond 450K, we observe a significant blue shift of the ODMR frequency that is correlated with the sample's phase transition to a disordered state.

The backpropagation algorithm, though effective for training neural networks, has a significant drawback: it mandates the sharing of weights. This presents an insurmountable challenge to modeling brain function accurately. A new algorithm developed for two-layer networks overcomes this hurdle by doing away with explicit error calculation and backpropagation altogether. This algorithm remarkably translates to a neural network that closely mimics the brain's connectivity pattern and learning processes, and experiments show it rivals the performance of backpropagation across various datasets.

Using field-theoretic methods, researchers studied a spin model on the triangular lattice, where the SU(3) representation was placed on each site, mimicking an antiferromagnetic Heisenberg spin model with p-box symmetry. Taking a large-p limit, they found the model reduces to a relativistic sigma model in three-dimensional space, described by the SU(3)/U(1)^2 manifold. Due to a non-trivial homotopy, this model possesses distinct magnetic vortices, or skyrmions, that monopole instantons can create and annihilate. Upon analyzing the Wess-Zumino term, researchers found the Berry phase associated with these monopoles causes interference, constraining possible Lagrangian perturbations by monopole operators, resulting in the degeneracy of VBS states for p not divisible by three. Researchers also investigated 't Hooft anomalies to establish constraints on the phase transitions of the system and discovered evidence supporting a phase transition between Néel and VBS phases.

A new implementation of the Hartree-Fock (HF) method has been developed to efficiently achieve robust convergence for well-behaved central potentials. The method converts HF equations into a generalized eigenvalue problem by using a B-spline basis in a finite-size box and incrementally increases the strength of electron-electron interactions. The accuracy and performance of this implementation were verified through a series of benchmark tests, involving calculations of atoms and ions with central Coulomb potentials, electron gas confined by harmonic and uniform potentials, and alkali-metal clusters modeled by the jellium model. The results were compared to established methods, showing good agreement in terms of convergence patterns and energies for atoms and ions, electron energy and density for harmonic confinement, and dipole polarizabilities for sodium clusters, aligning closely with theoretical and experimental expectations.

The distinction between orderly and chaotic behavior within complex networks of interdependent oscillators corresponds to varying functional states found in numerous applications, including active brain states and stable electrical grids. Researchers have lately shown substantial interest in explosive synchronization phenomena which enable sudden shifts between these states due to their rapid and drastic nature. Although previous studies have highlighted key attributes of complex systems capable of explosive synchronization, these analyses were primarily undertaken on a case-by-case basis. This work establishes an exact standard for identifying explosive synchronization within coupled oscillator ensembles by determining the critical relationship between disorder in their internal workings and structure. This breakthrough brings us closer to understanding the intricacies of complex systems responsible for abrupt transitions and dual stability in both living organisms and man-made systems.

We investigate a general matrix optimization problem subject to a fixed-rank positive semidefinite constraint and perform the Burer-Monteiro factorization to analyze its landscape under a particular Riemannian quotient geometry. Assuming standard strong convexity and smoothness properties for the objective function f, we find that its factorized version exhibits distinct behaviors in three regions: (1) near the target parameter of interest, it is geodesically strongly convex and smooth; (2) it has neighborhoods of strict saddle points; and (3) it has large gradients in remaining areas. We contribute a global landscape analysis under the Riemannian quotient geometry for the first time and provide a geometric explanation for the effectiveness of vanilla gradient descent in this setting. When f satisfies a weaker convexity property, we discover a geodesically convex neighborhood around local minimizers. We also analyze a particular case with no linear terms, providing a geometric explanation for why the algorithm converges to a specific solution.

A graph's edge coloring can be described as assigning different colors to edges based on a specific distance criterion, effectively mirroring the requirements of a certain vertex coloring in a transformed version of the graph.
